Low Back Pain in an Adult

red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Acute low back pain (under 4 weeks) with no red flag and a normal neurologic exam: no imaging. Treat with an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and tell the patient to stay active.

Read the past medical history before the population rule:

  • Prior cancer: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) with contrast; early vertebral metastasis is neurologically silent, so a normal neurologic exam does not remove the concern.
  • Urinary retention or saddle anesthesia: emergent MRI and decompression.
  • Upper motor neuron signs with known or suspected cancer (cord compression): dexamethasone first, then emergent whole-spine MRI.

Night pain that improves once the patient gets up is inflammatory; night pain unrelieved by moving, with age over 50, prior cancer or weight loss, is malignant.

Diagnosis
Red flags by category
CategoryRed flagsImaging
MalignancyPrior cancer, over 50, weight loss, night or rest pain, pain over 4 to 6 weeksMRI with contrast; radiograph plus ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) or CRP (C-reactive protein) if suspicion is moderate
InfectionFever, injection drug use, recent bacteremia, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedureMRI with contrast plus blood cultures
FractureOver 70, osteoporosis, chronic steroids, traumaRadiograph first
Cauda equina (emergency)Urinary retention (most sensitive), saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, reduced anal toneEmergent MRI and decompression
Cord compression (emergency)Upper motor neuron signs, hyperreflexia, sensory levelEmergent whole-spine MRI; dexamethasone first only when cancer is known or suspected
InflammatoryUnder 40, over 3 months, better with exercise, worse with rest, HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27)Sacroiliac (SI) joint radiograph, then MRI
Abdominal aortic aneurysmOver 60, atherosclerosis, pulsatile mass, tearing painUltrasound or CT (computed tomography) angiography
Inflammatory versus mechanical
InflammatoryMechanical
OnsetUnder 40, insidious, over 3 monthsAny age, often acute after an event
Night painSecond half of the nightUsually absent
Morning stiffnessOver 30 minutesUnder 30 minutes
Rest and activityWorse with rest, better with movementBetter with rest, worse with activity
NSAID responseDramaticVariable
Defining findings Inflammatory back pain – enthesitis, where tendons and ligaments insert into bone (rheumatoid arthritis causes synovitis instead) · Spondyloarthritis (PAIR) – psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease-associated, reactive; seronegative (rheumatoid factor negative), HLA-B27 associated; enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis · Ankylosing spondylitis – young men; HLA-B27 in about 90% (supportive, not diagnostic); sacroiliitis first; reduced Schober test and chest expansion, lost lumbar lordosis, late bamboo spine · Its complications – anterior uveitis (25 to 40%), aortitis with aortic regurgitation, AV (atrioventricular) block, apical pulmonary fibrosis, immunoglobulin A nephropathy, a rigid spine that fractures with minor trauma · Vertebral metastasis – seeds the vertebral body through the valveless Batson plexus; pedicle loss gives the winking owl sign; bone-seeking primaries “BLT (breast, lung, thyroid) with a Kosher (kidney) Pickle (prostate)”; plain films miss 30 to 50% of bone loss
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute low back pain
TierInterventionEscalate when
1NSAID and stay active, no bed rest; heat or a short muscle relaxant optionalNo better at 4 to 6 weeks, or a red flag appears
2Physical therapy (PT); MRI if radicular symptoms persistRadicular symptoms 6 weeks or more
3Epidural steroid injectionFailed conservative therapy
4Surgical referralProgressive deficit, cauda equina, refractory pain
By diagnosis Ankylosing spondylitis – NSAID and exercise, then a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) or interleukin-17 inhibitor; methotrexate and sulfasalazine help peripheral, not axial, disease; screen for latent tuberculosis before a TNF inhibitor · Malignant cord compression with deficits – dexamethasone before imaging, the one place treatment precedes diagnosis · Unstable aneurysm – straight to surgery
Why no imaging Early imaging brings more surgery without better outcomes. Asymptomatic disc bulges and degenerative change are near-universal by middle age, so a scan mostly finds incidental lesions that invite intervention. About 90% of acute low back pain and of sciatica resolves within 6 weeks.
Practice
  1. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of low back pain now pain down both legs cannot pass urine since this morning Numb over the buttocks and inner thighs Afebrile · bladder scan 800 mL · anal tone reduced → Emergent MRI + decompression → urinary retention and saddle anesthesia are cauda equina syndrome: emergent MRI and decompression
  2. 40-year-old man has 1 week of low back pain began 1 day after moving furniture tender over the paraspinal muscles, not the spine No fever, chills, constipation or urinary incontinence Afebrile · reflexes, strength and sensation normal → No imaging → acute pain with a mechanical cause and a history full of pertinent negatives needs no imaging: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and stay active
  3. 62-year-old woman has 6 weeks of low back pain treated for breast cancer 4 years ago worse at night, not relieved by rest Neurologic exam normal Afebrile · no weight loss → MRI for metastasis → prior cancer with night pain needs MRI with contrast even with a normal neurologic exam; plain films miss 30 to 50% of bone loss
  4. 72-year-old woman on chronic prednisone has sudden back pain began after a minor fall point tenderness over one midline lumbar vertebra No leg pain, numbness or weakness Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Vertebral compression fracture → age over 70, chronic steroids and a minor fall point to a vertebral compression fracture: lumbar radiograph first
  5. 47-year-old woman has 5 days of low back pain after gardening chronic kidney disease, stage 3 bleeding gastric ulcer last year No fever, weight loss or bladder change Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL · neurologic exam normal → Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID → same tier, a different agent: kidney disease and a prior bleed rule out an oral NSAID, so acetaminophen or a topical NSAID
  6. 47-year-old woman has 3 weeks of low back and left leg pain now cannot lift the front of her left foot foot slaps on walking No bladder or bowel change Afebrile · left ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 · saddle sensation normal → Urgent MRI → a new foot drop is a progressive deficit: urgent MRI, without the bladder or saddle signs that make it an emergency
  7. 55-year-old woman has 2 months of back pain that wakes her at night not relieved by getting up and moving lost 6 kg without trying Treated for breast cancer 3 years ago Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Metastasis → night pain unrelieved by moving, with prior cancer and weight loss, is metastasis, not inflammatory back pain: MRI
  8. 34-year-old man who injects drugs has 1 week of back pain fever and chills focal tenderness over one lumbar spinous process No leg weakness T 38.9 °C · erythrocyte sedimentation rate 98 mm/h → Vertebral osteomyelitis → fever with focal spinal tenderness in injection drug use is vertebral osteomyelitis: MRI with contrast plus blood cultures
  9. 47-year-old woman has 8 weeks of low back pain pain shoots down the lateral leg to the top of the foot no better with an NSAID No bladder change Afebrile · strength normal · left straight-leg raise positive → MRI, PT, consider epidural → radicular symptoms past 6 weeks: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and physical therapy (PT), with an epidural steroid injection if conservative care keeps failing
  10. 72-year-old man has 1 hour of sudden severe back pain pulsatile, tender mass above the umbilicus pale and light-headed Smoker with peripheral arterial disease and hypertension BP 82/50 mm Hg · HR 124/min → Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm → back pain with a pulsatile mass and hypotension is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: straight to surgery; do not delay for CT
  11. 68-year-old man has 1 year of buttock and leg pain when walking relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping cart cycles without pain No back pain at rest Afebrile · pedal pulses normal · strength normal → Spinal stenosis → leg pain on walking relieved by flexing forward, with normal pulses, is spinal stenosis
  12. 38-year-old man has 2 weeks of low back pain pain shoots below the right knee into the foot right straight-leg raise positive Began while lifting a sofa Afebrile · strength normal → Radiculopathy → pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise is radiculopathy
  13. 34-year-old man has 4 months of low back pain better with activity, worse with rest morning stiffness over 30 minutes Wakes in the second half of the night Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Inflammatory back pain → under 40, over 3 months, better with movement: inflammatory back pain; sacroiliac joint radiographs and HLA-B27
  14. 26-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain improves with exercise, worse after sitting morning stiffness for an hour Sacroiliac joint radiographs are normal Afebrile · reduced Schober test · chest expansion reduced → MRI of the SI joints → radiographs normal with suspicion still high: MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows active sacroiliitis first; HLA-B27 is supportive only
  15. 30-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis has a red, painful left eye began yesterday photophobia and blurred vision No discharge or itching Afebrile · small left pupil · redness greatest around the cornea → Anterior uveitis → the eye complication of spondyloarthritis is anterior uveitis: topical steroid and a cycloplegic
  16. 45-year-old man with a fused, bamboo-like spine for 15 years new exertional dyspnea diastolic murmur at the left sternal border No chest pain or syncope BP 150/50 mm Hg · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation from aortitis → aortitis widens the aortic root: aortic regurgitation
  17. 52-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis for 20 years new neck pain after a minor fall pain on any neck movement Old radiographs show a fused spine Afebrile · strength and sensation normal → Spinal fracture → a rigid spine is brittle: fracture after minor trauma, so CT (computed tomography) of the spine
  18. 24-year-old man has 1 week of a swollen right knee and left ankle bloody diarrhea 2 weeks ago red eyes and burning on urination No rash or nail changes T 37.8 °C · rheumatoid factor negative → Reactive arthritis → asymmetric lower-limb arthritis weeks after dysentery, with conjunctivitis and urethritis, is reactive arthritis
  19. 68-year-old man with diabetes has back stiffness radiograph: flowing ossification along the front of 4 or more vertebrae sacroiliac joints normal No morning stiffness over 30 minutes Afebrile · HLA-B27 negative → Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis → flowing anterior ossification with spared sacroiliac joints in an older man with diabetes is diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not spondyloarthritis
Common wrong answers Bed rest: harmful, delays recovery. CT of the lumbosacral spine: not indicated at 1 week, and MRI is the modality for disc and nerve root. Epidural injection: only after 4 to 6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone: does not improve acute sciatica.
Transferable rule

When most patients do not need a test, ask whether this patient is the exception. A dense list of pertinent negatives supports doing less. When a symptom fits two categories, its behavior separates them: here, what happens when the patient gets up.

Bipolar Disorder

rule out a cause, time the episode, then treatMania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize when needed to prevent harm: mania is an emergency.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine drug screen
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free thyroxine
  • CBC (complete blood count) and basic metabolic panel

Then time the episode:

  • Manic episode 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalized
  • Hypomanic episode 4 days or more in a row
  • Cyclothymic disorder 2 years or more of swings below episode criteria

One manic episode makes bipolar I disorder; psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization makes an episode manic, never hypomanic.

Treat: stop any antidepressant; start lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic.

Diagnosis
Manic episode criteria Mood – elevated, expansive or irritable mood plus more energy, most of the day, nearly every day · Duration – 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalization is necessary · Symptoms – 3 or more DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable · Severity – marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features · Cause – not a substance or medical condition; an episode that outlasts an antidepressant still counts · Mixed features – 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days of the episode
DIGFAST
  • Distractibility – attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli
  • Indiscretion – painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviours, foolish business investments
  • Grandiosity – inflated self-esteem
  • Flight of ideas – thoughts are racing
  • Activity increased – goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation
  • Sleep decreased – feels rested after only 3 hours
  • Talkativeness – pressure to keep talking
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute manic episode
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop antidepressants; lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic, alone or an antipsychotic plus lithium or valproateNo better after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses, adherence and substances checked
Add on or switchAnother first-line agent, added or switchedNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses
Severe or resistantElectroconvulsive therapyTop rung
By situation Severe agitation or psychosis – sedating second-generation antipsychotic, sometimes lorazepam; lithium takes 4 to 10 days · Could become pregnant – avoid valproate: teratogenic · After remission – continuous maintenance for years; lithium lowers suicide risk · Bipolar depression – suicide risk first; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone; no antidepressant alone
Practice
  1. 29-year-old man with 9 days of: 3-hour nights, rapid speech, new business plans is certain he can heal the sick with his touch Still works daily; major depressive episode 1 year ago Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → psychotic features make the episode manic by definition, even while he keeps working
  2. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of: sleeping 4 hours without fatigue faster speech and three new work projects Coworkers notice; she still meets deadlines; only past episode: major depression 2 years ago Elevated mood · no delusions · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar II disorder → 4 or more days of symptoms others notice, without marked impairment or psychosis, plus a past major depressive episode
  3. 35-year-old man admitted 4 months ago for a week of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech euthymic for 3 months on lithium at therapeutic levels asks to stop it now that he feels well BP 120/78 mm Hg → Continue lithium long term → maintenance for all patients with bipolar I disorder, continuous rather than intermittent
  4. 38-year-old woman with 10 days of irritable mood and: 2-hour nights, racing thoughts, nonstop talk $9,000 spent online; stopped going to work most days: crying, calling herself a terrible mother, thoughts of death Past admission for elevated mood Toxicology negative → Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with mixed features → irritable mood with 4 symptoms and marked impairment (stopped going to work) for 10 days, plus 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days; the past admission for elevated mood already makes it bipolar I
  5. 26-year-old woman on sertraline 4 weeks for depression; for 8 days she has: slept 3 hours a night, talked rapidly quit her job to launch three businesses; says she is destined for fame Euphoric mood · HR 92/min · pregnancy test negative → Stop sertraline and start quetiapine → a full manic episode on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start a first-line agent
  6. 33-year-old man found on his apartment roof at night announcing that he can fly 9 days of almost no sleep gave away his car; talks nonstop Refuses admission, saying he has never felt better Expansive mood · toxicology negative → Inpatient psychiatric admission → hospitalization is needed to prevent harm to himself; mania is an emergency; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  7. 29-year-old man in the emergency department shouting threats and throwing chairs at staff a week without sleep; pressured speech believes he is a secret agent chosen to save the world Similar hospitalization 2 years ago Irritable, expansive mood · toxicology negative → Sedating antipsychotic and lorazepam → severe manic psychosis compromising safety needs rapid behavioral control; lithium takes 4 to 10 days
  8. 41-year-old woman hospitalized with elevated mood, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lithium for 16 days, at therapeutic levels for 14 every dose confirmed She is no better Toxicology negative → Add quetiapine to lithium → no improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses with adherence and substance use checked: add on or switch
  9. 24-year-old woman admitted with 10 days of: little sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, reckless spending Elevated mood; no psychotic symptoms; sexually active with inconsistent condom use Pregnancy test negative · TSH normal · toxicology negative → Divalproex → valproate should not be used in a woman of childbearing potential (fetal malformations, impaired intellectual development)
  10. 27-year-old man brought in after walking into highway traffic, laughing 3 days without sleep savings spent on a sailboat; talks without pause Admitted for his own safety; no delusions; no earlier mood episodes Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → hospitalization satisfies both the duration and the severity criteria, so 3 days is enough
  11. 30-year-old woman with 3 weeks of: depressed mood, loss of interest, oversleeping, fatigue, poor concentration Hospitalized 2 years ago for 10 days of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and spending; no suicidal thoughts HR 72/min → Sertraline monotherapy → antidepressant monotherapy is not used in bipolar I depression and risks a switch to mania; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone is first line
  12. 45-year-old man on lithium for 6 years after two admissions for euphoria, grandiosity and no sleep 2 weeks of depressed mood, insomnia, poor appetite, slowed movements, hopelessness says his family would be better off without him HR 76/min → Assess suicide risk → most suicide deaths in bipolar disorder occur in the depressive phase, so suicide risk comes first
  13. 36-year-old woman with 8 days of: little sleep, restlessness, rapid speech, irritability 4-kg weight loss over 6 weeks; always feels hot Fine tremor of the outstretched hands HR 118/min · toxicology negative → Serum TSH and free thyroxine → weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia and tremor point to hyperthyroidism, a medical cause of these symptoms
How NBME framed it: question 1

24-year-old receptionist at an accounting firm brought in by police cursed at a rental car agent; grew “out of control” when no luxury sports car was available asks for the physician’s number, winks, promises “a good time” and tries a kiss agitated; feels “absolutely fantastic”; loud, rapid speech says she is obviously very rich and the agents will regret delaying her for a television interview Examination normal · urine toxicology negative

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): hyperactive and impulsive; but ADHD is chronic and in more than one setting, and this is acute.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed grandiose belief; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and she has it.
  • Histrionic personality disorder: the wink and the attempted kiss; but personality disorders are chronic and pervasive.
  • Schizophrenia: a grandiose delusion; but it sits inside a manic episode (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder or histrionic personality disorder. Bipolar disorder: the seductiveness sits inside an acute episode of euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, overspending and grandiosity. (NBME gives no duration; it reads the severity and psychosis as mania.)

How NBME framed it: question 2

43-year-old man admitted with superficial frostbite of the toes police found him 5 hours earlier walking barefoot in a snowstorm says he is a god who can melt snow and purify the heart knows the date and place asked to recall red, penny, train, he playfully laughs: “color, coin, conveyance” rapid, incessant speech; paces with arms raised, both index fingers aimed upward Normal vital signs and laboratory results

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute delusion; but his psychosis is secondary to mania.
  • Delirium, alcohol withdrawal: found wandering in the cold; but vital signs are normal and he is fully oriented.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed delusion; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and he has it.
  • Malingering: an odd, dangerous act; but nobody walks into frostbite for gain, and he has none.
  • Schizoid personality disorder: an odd man; but he is playful and talkative, not detached.
  • Schizophrenia: the god delusion and the posture; but the delusion is part of mania (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder, manic, or schizophrenia. Bipolar disorder, manic: the god delusion rides on playful, euphoric affect, rapid incessant speech and pacing; NBME also cites no negative symptoms.

Pairs with Psychosis: does the psychosis occur only during a mood episode? Lithium Therapy: what does maintenance lithium do to the kidney and thyroid? Delirium: are attention and orientation intact? Part I Thyroid Disease in an Adult: is a thyroid cause driving the energy and weight loss?
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychosis or a personality disorder, rule out a drug or thyroid cause, then ask whether the symptoms sit inside a discrete episode of elevated or irritable mood with DIGFAST symptoms; if they do, it is mania, and any antidepressant stops.

Bone Lesions in a Child

childhood bone lesions by site · age and periosteum · what each does next · imaging before biopsy · Ewing or infectionWhere does it sit, how old is the child, and is the periosteum quiet or aggressive?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Read the plain film by site and periosteum; then recall what that lesion does next.

  • Painless hard bump near a joint, spur continuous with the cortex and medulla: osteochondroma. It grows until the physes close, then stops. Observe; no biopsy. About 1% of solitary lesions turn malignant.
  • Night pain relieved by NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), small lucent nidus: osteoid osteoma. It involutes over years.
  • Central metaphyseal lucency, no periosteal reaction: unicameral bone cyst. Observe with serial films; the risk is fracture.
  • Sunburst periosteum, often with a Codman triangle, in a metaphysis: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft, pelvis or spine, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma.

Night pain that wakes the child, with fever or weight loss, points to malignancy, not a benign lesion.

An aggressive film gets MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) before biopsy; chest CT (computed tomography) stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor: Ewing sarcoma can raise the ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and WBC (white blood cell count).

Diagnosis
Where it sits, and the clue
LesionSiteAge and clue
ChondroblastomaEpiphysisTeens, physes open; well-defined lucency, thin sclerotic rim
Giant cell tumorEpiphysisOver 20, mature; soap bubble
OsteochondromaMetaphysisTeens; most common benign; painless spur; multiple if hereditary
Unicameral bone cystMetaphysis (humerus, femur)Physes open; painless, incidental; central lucency, no periosteal reaction
OsteosarcomaMetaphysisTeens; sunburst; high ALP (alkaline phosphatase); rarely febrile
Osteoid osteomaLong bone (often proximal femur) or spineTeens; night pain gone with NSAIDs; nidus
Ewing sarcomaShaft, pelvis, axialPeak 10 to 15; may be febrile; onion skin
ChondrosarcomaPelvis, proximal femur or humerusAdults over 40 to 50
Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis Ewing – weeks; shaft, pelvis or spine; small round blue cells · Osteomyelitis – days; long-bone metaphysis; trauma or immunodeficiency support it when present; inflammatory cells and necrotic bone
Management and treatment
By lesion Observe – osteochondroma; unicameral bone cyst with serial films; osteoid osteoma with NSAIDs · Curettage – chondroblastoma and giant cell tumor, both locally aggressive; giant cell tumor has high local recurrence · Malignant – osteosarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection; Ewing sarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection, radiation or both
Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, 5 weeks of worsening left hip pain stairs hard intermittent fever, fatigue; no trauma or chronic illness Warm, tender left iliac crest swelling T 38.3 °C, other vitals normal · lucent ilium, layered periosteum · biopsy: small round blue cells → Ewing sarcoma → a pelvic lytic lesion over weeks with layered periosteum is Ewing sarcoma: MRI maps it, and biopsy shows uniform small round blue cells in sheets, little cytoplasm, fibrous septa; osteomyelitis favors long bones over days, and osteosarcoma is metaphyseal, rarely pelvic and rarely febrile
  2. 13-year-old girl, painless hard bump above the left knee 3 weeks; unchanged no trauma, fever or weight loss Firm, nontender distal femoral mass Vital signs normal · film: metaphyseal spur pointing away from the joint, continuous with cortex and medulla → Grows until the growth plates close, then stops → a spur continuous with the cortex and medulla is an osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumor: it grows with the skeleton until physeal closure, then stops; transformation is about 1% and involution belongs to osteoid osteoma
  3. 15-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain worst at night; unrelated to activity ibuprofen relieves it completely No weight loss or limp Afebrile · film: small round lucency with a sclerotic rim, proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain relieved by NSAIDs with a small lucent nidus in a sclerotic rim is osteoid osteoma, most often in the proximal femur
  4. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the femur 2 months ago night pain controlled by ibuprofen no other complaints Parents ask what happens if nothing more is done Afebrile · repeat film unchanged → Spontaneous involution → osteoid osteoma involutes on its own over years, so NSAIDs and serial films are reasonable
  5. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the tibia last week pain wakes him at night one ibuprofen dose stops it within an hour Parents ask why the medicine works so well Afebrile · nidus under 2 cm on film → Prostaglandin production by the nidus → the nidus makes prostaglandins, which NSAIDs block, so the response is nearly diagnostic
  6. 13-year-old girl with 6 weeks of worsening pain below the knee firm mass over the proximal tibia no trauma Pain now present at rest Afebrile · film: mixed lytic and dense metaphyseal lesion, sunburst periosteal reaction → Osteosarcoma → a metaphyseal mixed lesion with a sunburst reaction in a teenager is osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy of childhood; prior radiation and hereditary retinoblastoma raise the risk
  7. 15-year-old boy with 6 weeks of progressive pain above the right knee now wakes him at night firm, tender distal thigh swelling Film: ill-defined mixed lytic-sclerotic distal femoral metaphysis Afebrile · sunburst reaction, Codman triangle · ALP elevated → MRI of the right femur → an aggressive film gets MRI of the affected bone before biopsy: it maps soft tissue and vessels and plans the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs
  8. 12-year-old boy with 6 weeks of worsening thigh pain wakes him at night intermittent fevers; lost 2 kg; no trauma or recent infection Film: moth-eaten mid-shaft femoral lysis, onion-skin periosteum T 38.2 °C · ESR 55 mm/h → Ewing sarcoma → a permeative diaphyseal lesion with onion-skin layers over weeks, with weight loss, is Ewing sarcoma; the shaft and the 6-week course argue against osteomyelitis; fever, when present, often means it has spread
  9. 7-year-old boy, febrile 4 days won't bear weight on left leg warm, point-tender distal femoral metaphysis; full, painless knee motion MRI: marrow edema, small subperiosteal collection T 39.2 °C · WBC 16,000/mm³, neutrophils · hemoglobin, platelets normal · CRP markedly high · film normal → Osteomyelitis → days of fever with metaphyseal point tenderness and an early normal film is osteomyelitis: blood culture, intravenous antibiotics, drain the abscess; Ewing sarcoma runs for weeks
  10. 9-year-old boy with arm pain after a minor fall no pain before the fall tender upper arm Fracture through a well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency Afebrile · thin sclerotic margin; no periosteal reaction → Unicameral bone cyst → a central metaphyseal lucency with no periosteal reaction that fractures is a unicameral bone cyst; medullary expansion thins the cortex; chondroblastoma is also a lucency with a sclerotic rim, but it sits in the epiphysis
  11. 10-year-old girl, mild shoulder pain after a fall on an outstretched hand full range of motion no weight loss No fracture on film Afebrile · incidental well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency · thin cortex; narrow transition; no periosteal reaction → Observation with serial radiographs → an incidental unicameral bone cyst is observed with serial films; it resolves by physeal closure, and the risk is pathologic fracture
  12. 28-year-old woman with 4 months of knee pain and swelling skeletally mature no trauma, fever or weight loss Eccentric expansile lytic lesion of the distal femoral epiphysis Afebrile · soap-bubble appearance on film → Giant cell tumor of bone → an expansile soap-bubble epiphyseal lesion after skeletal maturity is giant cell tumor: locally destructive, curettage or excision, high local recurrence
  13. 16-year-old boy with 3 months of constant knee pain physes still open; no weight loss mild joint swelling Well-circumscribed epiphyseal lucency, thin sclerotic rim, crossing the physis Afebrile · no periosteal reaction → Chondroblastoma → an epiphyseal lucency before skeletal maturity is chondroblastoma; age separates it from giant cell tumor; curettage
Pairs with Leg Pain in a Child: one-sided night pain needs a film. Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans: the post-injury mass. Acute Leukemia in a Child: bone pain from marrow. The Limping Child: the febrile limp.
Transferable rule

To predict a lesion's course, name it first, then recall what it does. To name it, check site, age and fever before reading the film.

Infectious Diarrhea

timing gates · organism by food source · stool culture, blood culture or neither · who gets an antibioticWhat did the patient eat, how soon did it start, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?

Source vignette Pt – 14-year-old girl with 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, today with fever and blood in the stool; home from a week-long summer camp, well while there; CVID on immunoglobulin replacement; sinusitis a month ago treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate · Exam – T 38.2 C, HR 102; mild diffuse tenderness, no peritoneal signs · Labs – stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella · Q – the most likely underlying cause of her illness; options spanned food handling, seafood, contaminated infusions, antibiotic disruption of gut flora and typhoid vaccine failure
The decision point

Identify the organism from the exposure. Nontyphoidal Salmonella comes from undercooked poultry and eggs. Food left unrefrigerated lets it multiply. Symptoms start within 3 days with fever, vomiting, cramps and diarrhea, which can be bloody in children. Camp food fits this source, and her stool culture confirms Salmonella.

The organism then determines the workup and treatment. Invasive diarrhea needs a stool culture. A fever-first illness after travel is typhoid and needs a blood culture. Most bacterial diarrhea needs only rehydration.

Timing gates 1 to 6 hours, vomiting first, no fever – preformed toxin: S aureus or B cereus · Within about 3 days, fever and diarrhea – invasive bacteria: nontyphoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella; Shiga toxin E coli with little fever · Fever for days to weeks after travel, diarrhea minor – typhoid · During or after antibiotics, watery – C difficile
Diarrhea by source: the differential
OrganismSource and settingThe NBME tellTest and treatment
Nontyphoidal SalmonellaUndercooked poultry and eggs, poor refrigeration; reptiles and backyard poultryFever, vomiting, cramps; bloody stools possible in childrenStool culture; supportive; antibiotics only for infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia
Typhoid (S Typhi)Travel to areas with poor sanitation; contaminated food or waterFever and bacteremia first; abdominal pain, rose spots, relative bradycardia; later splenomegaly, intestinal perforationBlood culture; ceftriaxone; the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains
CampylobacterUndercooked poultry, unpasteurized milkFever, bloody diarrhea, pain that can mimic appendicitis; Guillain-Barre weeks laterStool culture; supportive unless severe or prolonged
Shiga toxin E coli (O157:H7)Undercooked ground beef, petting zoosBloody diarrhea with little fever; HUS about a week laterStool culture and Shiga toxin test; no antibiotics, no antimotility drugs
ShigellaDay care; spreads person to person from a very small inoculumHigh fever, bloody diarrhea, seizures in young childrenStool culture; azithromycin shortens illness and spread
Vibrio parahaemolyticusRaw or undercooked seafood, shellfishWatery diarrhea and cramps after raw oystersSupportive
S aureus and B cereus toxinToxin already in the food: S aureus in ham, mayonnaise or custard; B cereus in reheated riceVomiting within 1 to 6 hours, no fever, several diners illClinical; supportive
C difficileRecent antibioticsWatery diarrhea at onset, cramps, leukocytosisStool toxin or PCR; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Stool culture, with Shiga toxin testing if bloodyFirstNames the organismFor fever with bloody diarrhea, immunocompromise, severe or prolonged illness, or an outbreak
Blood cultureBy branchS Typhi or other bacteremiaFever-first illness after travel, infants under 3 months, immunocompromise
C difficile toxin or PCRBy branchPositiveWatery diarrhea during or after antibiotics
Stool ova and parasites or Giardia antigenBy branchGiardiaProlonged watery, greasy diarrhea after untreated water; common in CVID and IgA deficiency
Stool studies for brief watery diarrhea without fever or bloodSkip Self-limited; rehydrate
Scenario bank
  1. 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated → Blood culture and antibiotic therapy → infants under 3 months with Salmonella are at risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they are treated
  2. 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella → Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggs → nontyphoidal Salmonella from undercooked poultry or eggs starts within 3 days, and warmth lets it multiply; bloody stools are common in children
  3. 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia → Bacillus cereus food poisoning → vomiting within hours from a toxin already in the food; reheated rice is the classic source; supportive care
  4. 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs → Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection → raw or undercooked shellfish; self-limited, supportive care
  5. 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending → Oral azithromycin → antibiotics and antimotility drugs raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome in Shiga toxin E coli infection; rehydrate and watch hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine
  6. 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable → Blood cultures → typhoid presents as fever and bacteremia; the blood culture confirms it before empiric ceftriaxone
  7. 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella → Oral rehydration and supportive care → antibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella in a healthy child and prolong carriage
Management Rehydrate first – oral rehydration for nearly everyone · Antibiotics only for – typhoid; Shigella; C difficile; nontyphoidal Salmonella in infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia, since treating others prolongs carriage · Suspected Shiga toxin E coli – never antibiotics or antimotility drugs, which raise the risk of HUS
Pearls Exposures to know: a pet turtle, reheated rice, raw oysters, a hamburger · Humoral immunodeficiency such as CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) raises the risk of Salmonella, Campylobacter and Giardia infection; it does not change which food carries which organism · A vaccine exists for typhoid, not for nontyphoidal Salmonella · In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is the organism of osteomyelitis, which is why these children are treated
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers CVID (common variable immunodeficiency): are IgG and at least one other isotype low, with poor vaccine responses? Part I Right Lower Quadrant Pain covers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and its list of who gets antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
Transferable rule In infectious diarrhea, name the organism from the exposure and the timing. That organism then determines the culture and whether to treat. A risk factor for a different organism is not the exposure.
Salient decoyAntibiotic disruption of gut flora: the recent amoxicillin-clavulanate is real, but it predisposes to C difficile, which starts watery; the culture grew Salmonella.
Class-vs-memberTyphoid vaccine failure: the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains, and there is no vaccine for nontyphoidal Salmonella; CVID blunting the response does not matter here.
True-fact-wrong-slotRaw or unrefrigerated seafood: a real foodborne source, but of Vibrio parahaemolyticus, not Salmonella.
Salient decoyContaminated immunoglobulin infusions: rare, and they cause bacteremia with high fever and chills found on blood culture, not gastroenteritis with a positive stool culture.

Congenital Infections (TORCH)

organism first, then its signature sequela · where calcifications sit · rubella triad · parvovirus · herpes without vesiclesWhere are the calcifications, and what is that organism's signature sequela?

Source vignette Pt – 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly · Imaging – periventricular calcifications · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital cytomegalovirus, congenital toxoplasmosis and congenital rubella
The decision point

Identify the organism, then its signature sequela.

Calcifications along the ventricular margin (periventricular) indicate CMV (cytomegalovirus). Calcifications scattered through the parenchyma indicate toxoplasmosis. An indoor cat suggests toxoplasmosis but is compatible with congenital CMV.

Defining criteria Periventricular calcifications – CMV · Diffuse parenchymal calcifications – toxoplasmosis, with chorioretinitis · Subcortical calcifications with arthrogryposis – Zika · Diagnostic window – urine or saliva PCR (polymerase chain reaction) within the first 3 weeks of life, after which congenital and perinatal acquisition cannot be separated; later, a positive PCR on the stored newborn dried blood spot may help, but a negative does not exclude it
Congenital infection – the differential
InfectionIllness scriptThe NBME tell
CMVMost common congenital infection; hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephalyPeriventricular calcifications with microcephaly; sequela is sensorineural hearing loss
ToxoplasmosisCat litter, undercooked meatDiffuse parenchymal calcifications and chorioretinitis; sequela is obstructive hydrocephalus
RubellaUnvaccinated motherCataracts and a continuous machine-like PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) murmur
SyphilisUntreated maternal infectionSnuffles, palm-and-sole rash, periostitis; no CNS (central nervous system) calcifications
HSV (herpes simplex virus) Can't missIntrapartum acquisitionDays 5 to 21, vesicles, seizures, temporal lobe; without vesicles, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with lymphocytes and red cells and normal glucose
ZikaMaternal travelSevere microcephaly with subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis
Parvovirus B19Maternal febrile illness with arthralgia; risk highest before 20 weeksHydrops fetalis or fetal loss; congenital anomalies are rare in survivors; follow with serial ultrasonography and MCA (middle cerebral artery) Doppler
Listeria monocytogenes Can't missNonspecific maternal febrile illness, often foodborneSevere neonatal sepsis with disseminated abscesses in liver, spleen, lung, kidney and brain
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Head ultrasound or CT (computed tomography)FirstPeriventricular calcificationsCMV; diffuse parenchymal: toxoplasmosis; subcortical with arthrogryposis: Zika
Saliva CMV PCR, first 3 weeksScreenPositiveNeeds urine PCR to confirm; saliva gives false positives
Urine CMV PCR, first 3 weeksConfirmsPositiveCongenital CMV; after 3 weeks, perinatal acquisition cannot be excluded
Dilated eye examBy branchChorioretinitis, or cataractsChorioretinitis with diffuse calcifications: toxoplasmosis; cataracts: rubella
Infant rubella IgMBy branchPositiveCongenital rubella syndrome; serology, not PCR
Cerebrospinal fluid herpes simplex virus PCRBy branchPositiveNeonatal herpes encephalitis; start intravenous acyclovir before the result
Serial audiology through childhoodStagingSensorineural hearing loss, often late-onsetCMV's main sequela; a passed newborn screen does not end follow-up
Infant CMV IgGSkipMaternal IgG crosses the placentaCannot separate infant from maternal antibody
Mnemonic TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex virus
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn with a positive saliva CMV PCR → Confirm with urine PCR → saliva gives false positives
  2. 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly, periventricular calcifications → Congenital CMV → valganciclovir
  3. 2 mo F with symptomatic congenital CMV, greatest long-term risk → Sensorineural hearing loss
  4. Newborn with diffuse parenchymal calcifications, chorioretinitis and ventriculomegaly → Congenital toxoplasmosis
  5. Newborn with cataracts and a continuous machine-like murmur → Congenital rubella
  6. Newborn with snuffles, a palm-and-sole rash and long-bone periostitis → Congenital syphilis → penicillin
  7. 7 yo with notched incisors, saddle nose and interstitial keratitis → Late congenital syphilis
  8. Neonate on day 10 with vesicles, seizures and temporal-lobe changes → Neonatal HSV → intravenous acyclovir
  9. Newborn with severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis after maternal travel → Congenital Zika
  10. Newborn with suspected congenital CMV → Urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks of life
  11. Newborn with symptomatic congenital CMV, treatment duration → 6 Months of valganciclovir
  12. Newborn with congenital CMV who passes the newborn hearing screen → Serial audiology through childhood → the loss is often late-onset
  13. Infant with congenital CMV and enlarged ventricles → Hydrocephalus ex vacuo → parenchymal volume loss
  14. 2-day-old, failed hearing screen bilaterally, absent red reflex, continuous murmur at the left second interspace, hepatosplenomegaly, growth below the 5th percentile, mother with a first-trimester febrile illness and arthralgia → Congenital rubella syndrome → hearing loss, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus
  15. Why the first trimester is rubella's dangerous window → Transplacental infection during organogenesis → spontaneous abortion or congenital rubella syndrome
  16. Newborn with suspected congenital rubella syndrome; establishing the diagnosis → Infant rubella IgM serology → serology rather than PCR, because the PCR window belongs to cytomegalovirus
  17. Pregnant woman with fever and arthralgia at 16 weeks whose fetus develops ascites, effusions and skin edema → Parvovirus B19 with hydrops fetalis → anomalies are rare in survivors
  18. 29 yo woman at 18 weeks' gestation, an elementary school teacher, exposed during a school outbreak of slapped-cheek rash; she has mild arthralgia; parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; ultrasound today shows a normally grown fetus without hydrops → Serial ultrasound with MCA Doppler → Acute maternal parvovirus B19 infection; watch for fetal anemia and hydrops
  19. 26 yo woman at 14 weeks' gestation whose 5-year-old has a slapped-cheek facial rash and lacy rash on the arms; she has had fatigue and aching wrists and knees for 3 days → Parvovirus B19 IgM → Acute maternal infection; then serial fetal ultrasonography
  20. 31 yo woman at 23 weeks' gestation with confirmed acute parvovirus B19 infection 4 weeks ago, followed with serial ultrasonography; middle cerebral artery Doppler now indicates severe fetal anemia, and there is new fetal ascites and skin edema → Intrauterine transfusion → Hydrops fetalis from parvovirus B19 fetal anemia
  21. 8-day-old girl with apnea during a feed, then a focal seizure with bicycling leg movements and eye deviation; lethargic and hypotonic with brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski signs; cerebrospinal fluid glucose 55 mg/dL, protein 65 mg/dL, 350 erythrocytes/mm3, 70 leukocytes/mm3 with 80% lymphocytes; empiric antibiotics started → Herpes simplex virus → confirm with cerebrospinal fluid PCR and add intravenous acyclovir
  22. 10-day-old boy with lethargy and a focal seizure and no skin lesions; cerebrospinal fluid shows normal glucose, mildly raised protein, 90 leukocytes/mm3 that are mostly lymphocytes, and many erythrocytes; empiric antibiotics are running → Add intravenous acyclovir now → empiric antiviral therapy before the PCR result
  23. 12-day-old with poor feeding, lethargy and focal seizures; cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with many erythrocytes and normal glucose → CSF HSV PCR → neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis
Shared sequela Rubella also causes sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss therefore does not separate rubella from CMV (cytomegalovirus); the calcification pattern does.
The rubella triad Sensorineural hearing loss – a failed newborn hearing screen · Cataracts – an absent red reflex, or leukocoria · Patent ductus arteriosus – a continuous machine-like murmur at the left second interspace · Plus – growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and a purpuric blueberry-muffin rash · Maternal arthralgia after a febrile illness in pregnancy – rubella causes organ malformation from first-trimester organogenesis; parvovirus B19 causes hydrops and no malformation
Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy Exposure – a child with slapped cheeks at home, school or day care; a child with the rash is no longer contagious, so exposure happened earlier; most maternal infections are asymptomatic, others flu-like with rash or symmetric arthralgia · Maternal serology – B19 IgM positive means acute infection; IgG positive with IgM negative means past infection and immunity; B19 DNA testing if immunocompromised · Fetal risk – the virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the danger is fetal anemia, then hydrops or fetal death, not malformation · Acute infection – serial ultrasonography with middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect fetal anemia and hydrops · Severe fetal anemia – intrauterine transfusion
Neonatal herpes without vesicles Timing – seizures, lethargy or apnea in the second or third week of life; vesicles are often absent · Cerebrospinal fluid – normal or mildly low glucose, mildly raised protein, a modest pleocytosis that is mostly lymphocytes, and many red cells · Bacterial meningitis – low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant leukocyte count, often over 1,000/mm3 · Confirm – herpes simplex virus PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of the cerebrospinal fluid · Treat – add intravenous acyclovir to empiric antibiotics without waiting for the PCR · How NBME framed it: no vesicles are given and antibiotics are already begun, so the day of life and the lymphocytic, bloody cerebrospinal fluid identify the virus.
Pearls CMV (cytomegalovirus) is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss · Only about 10% are symptomatic at birth, and that group carries up to 50% hearing-loss risk untreated · Six months of valganciclovir is better than six weeks: 8% versus 13% hearing worsening at one year · Hearing loss is progressive and can be late-onset, so passing the newborn screen does not discharge the child from audiology · CMV – ventricles enlarge ex vacuo from volume loss · Toxoplasmosis – ventricles enlarge from obstruction
Pairs with Part I Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease covers the childhood sensorineural causes. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the same imaging; the calcification pattern and the white-matter injury each point to a different cause. Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn: does the cerebrospinal fluid show low glucose with over 1,000 neutrophil-predominant leukocytes, or lymphocytes and red cells with normal glucose?
Transferable rule Identifying the complication of a syndrome takes two independent steps: name the syndrome, then its complication. When anatomic distribution and exposure history are both given, always rely on anatomic distribution.
Unchecked attributeCytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis both follow a mild maternal flu-like illness, but neither produces cataracts or a cardiac defect. The maternal history is shared; the fetal organ pattern separates them.
Salient decoyToxoplasmosis: the indoor cat suggests it, but a cat is also compatible with cytomegalovirus.
True-fact-wrong-slotRubella: it causes cataracts, but not periventricular calcifications.
Salient decoyGroup B streptococcus: the antibiotics already begun point toward it, but neonatal bacterial meningitis gives low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant count, often over 1,000/mm3.
Unchecked attributeEscherichia coli: a common cause of neonatal meningitis, but a count of 70 that is mostly lymphocytes, with normal glucose, does not fit a bacterial cause.
True-fact-wrong-slotCytomegalovirus: symptomatic congenital infection shows at birth with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, not as an acute encephalitis in the second week.
True-fact-wrong-slotToxoplasma gondii: congenital infection shows chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, not a new encephalitis on day 8.

edits.html:
Enuresis

1° vs 2° · mono- vs nonmonosymptomatic · urinalysis and exam · alarm vs desmopressinHas the urine been tested, and what has been tried, for how long?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Bedwetting at least twice weekly for at least 3 months, or with clinically significant distress or impairment, from age 5 (or an equivalent developmental level) is enuresis. Every child gets an examination and a urinalysis first, primary or secondary; a stressor never replaces them.

Classify on two axes:

  • Primary: never dry for 6 months; usually maturational.
  • Secondary: dry 6 months or more, now wetting; look for a cause.
  • Monosymptomatic: bedwetting only.
  • Nonmonosymptomatic: daytime urgency or holding; treat constipation and daytime symptoms first. A weak stream or dribbling in a boy points to urethral valves.

Normal workup, nothing tried: education, reassurance and motivational therapy. Then an alarm for a durable cure, or desmopressin for a fast, event-driven effect.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Enuresis – bedwetting at least twice weekly for at least 3 months, or with clinically significant distress or impairment, at age 5 or older (or an equivalent developmental level) · Secondary – 6 months or more of continuous dryness, then wetting again · Nonmonosymptomatic – daytime lower urinary tract symptoms with the bedwetting
Management and treatment
Management ladder: monosymptomatic enuresis, no cause found
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Education, reassurance, motivational therapy (reward effort and routine, not dry nights); treat constipation; void every 3 hours while awake and before bed; no drinks 1 to 2 hours before bed, drink well in the morning3 to 6 months without improvement, and the child or family is bothered
2Alarm: best long-term cure; needs a motivated family; usually offered over age 6; consider stopping after 14 consecutive dry nights, restart on relapse.
Or desmopressin: works fast, for camp or sleepovers; relapses more; limit evening fluids, none from 1 hour before the dose until 8 hours after (with oral dosing, hyponatremia is rare)		Alarm without improvement after 6 weeks: add or switch. Failure of both: tier 3
3Imipramine rarely (cardiotoxic in overdose); oxybutynin only with desmopressin or imipramine, not alone; urology referralTop rung
By diagnosis Under 5 – reassure; below the diagnostic age · Secondary – treat the cause; with no cause found, use the ladder · Desmopressin toxicity – headache, vomiting, seizure: hyponatremia; stop the drug; any neurologic symptoms: hypertonic saline; no symptoms: strict water restriction · Why the alarm lasts – conditioning survives stopping it; desmopressin's effect does not
Practice
  1. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly has never had a dry night dry by day since age 4, no urgency or dribbling Nothing tried yet; three siblings were dry by age 3 Afebrile · examination normal · urinalysis normal · glucose 82 mg/dL → Education, reassurance and motivational therapy → primary and monosymptomatic with a normal workup and nothing tried: start on the first rung; desmopressin skips a tier, and 2 pm is the wrong hour (limit the evening, drink well in the morning); siblings dry by 3 is a parental comparison, not a clue, while a family history of enuresis would support a maturational cause
  2. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed nightly for 4 months was dry at night for 2 years no daytime urgency, dysuria or dribbling Otherwise healthy Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · examination normal → Secondary enuresis → 6 months or more of dryness before the wetting makes it secondary; a cause is sought, and the urinalysis comes first
  3. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 3 weeks was dry at night for a year began after her parents separated Parents ask for counseling only Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg · examination normal → Obtain the urinalysis first → a plausible stressor never replaces the urinalysis; one cheap test screens the organic causes, then address the stressor
  4. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 2 weeks after a year dry drinking far more than usual tired, with 2 kg of weight loss No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: glucose 3+, ketones 1+, specific gravity 1.030 → New-onset diabetes mellitus → glucosuria with ketones in new wetting is type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise: serum glucose and HbA1c (hemoglobin A1c)
  5. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a week after a year dry also has new daytime accidents No complaint of burning, and no stressor at home T 37.8 °C · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, no glucose → Urinary tract infection → a urinary infection can present as new wetting without dysuria in a child: urine culture, then treat
  6. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a month after a year dry drinks water through the night large pale voids No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: specific gravity 1.002, no glucose, no leukocytes → Diabetes insipidus → a very low specific gravity in new wetting points to diabetes insipidus: a water deprivation test, then the desmopressin response
  7. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly has daytime urgency and squats on her heel to hold urine stools hard, every 4 days Never dry at night Afebrile · examination: stool palpable in the left lower quadrant → Nonmonosymptomatic enuresis → daytime symptoms make it nonmonosymptomatic: bladder diary, and treat the constipation first, which is often curative
  8. 7-year-old girl still wets the bed most nights 8 months of reward charts and a voiding routine family distressed and keen to keep trying Dry by day; no constipation Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Enuresis alarm → tier 1 has failed past 3 to 6 months in a bothered, motivated family: the alarm gives the most durable cure
  9. 6-year-old girl who has never been dry at night goes to sleepaway camp next week 4 months of reward charts have helped only a little Dry by day; no constipation; parents want a quick fix Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Desmopressin → event-driven beats durable: desmopressin works within days; the alarm needs weeks; oxybutynin is not used alone
  10. 6-year-old girl taking desmopressin for wetting the bed has headache and vomiting had a seizure an hour ago drank several cups of juice at a party tonight Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · serum sodium pending → Hyponatremia → desmopressin is an ADH (antidiuretic hormone) analog; free-water retention gives both its effect and its hyponatremic seizures: stop it; a seizure needs hypertonic saline
  11. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly and dribbles by day weak urinary stream dribbling after voiding Never dry at night; no constipation or urgency Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg · examination otherwise normal → Posterior urethral valves → a weak stream or dribbling in a boy is posterior urethral valves until proven otherwise: renal ultrasound and VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram)
  12. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly and now has daytime accidents a tuft of hair over the sacrum brisk lower-extremity reflexes Dry by day from age 3 until this year; no constipation Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg · urinalysis normal → Spinal MRI → a sacral tuft with abnormal neurology is spinal dysraphism: spinal MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), not reassurance
  13. 4-year-old boy wets the bed most nights dry during the day, no urgency or constipation Parents are worried because his cousin was dry at 3 and ask about medicine Afebrile · growth normal · examination normal → Reassurance → enuresis is not diagnosed before age 5: reassure, since many children become dry without treatment
Pairs with Polyuria covers the next step once a very low specific gravity points to diabetes insipidus: the water deprivation test, what its result means, and the one child in whom it must not be done. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule

Set the tier by what has been done and for how long: a normal workup means no further testing, and no treatment yet means no escalation. Pick the lowest rung not yet exhausted.

Seizure with Fever in a Child

benign only inside the age window · intracranial signs · fontanelle and tone, not the neck · when to tapIs the child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Source vignette Pt – 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone · Q – the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge
The decision point

At 10 weeks old, febrile seizure is excluded by age. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years. A child outside that window with fever and a seizure needs a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently indicate the same step. A full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure. The drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. A supple neck is not reassuring, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants; read the fontanelle and the tone instead. Perform a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Simple febrile seizure – age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging · Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture – age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease · Additional considerations for tapping – current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history · The open-fontanelle exemption – signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head computed tomography (CT) first
Pertinent positives & negatives Age 10 weeks – outside the febrile-seizure window entirely; this alone rules out discharge · Full anterior fontanelle – a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image · Fontanelle open – acts as a pop-off valve, so CT is not needed first · Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure – a postictal period beyond 10 minutes. This is prolonged altered mental status and an indication on its own · Weak suck and decreased tone – altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation · Neck supple – excludes nothing, because meningeal signs can be subtle or absent under 12 months · Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped – no benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes. No EEG (electroencephalography), since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent · Skin normal – no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation; four other findings already indicate the tap · Vaccinations up to date – the incomplete-immunization consideration no longer applies, but the indication for the tap remains
Seizure with fever in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tellExcluded here by
Bacterial meningitis Can't missAny age, and infants localize poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signsSeizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture decidingNone (the answer to pursue)
Simple febrile seizureViral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal childAge 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examinationAge 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle
Complex febrile seizureThe same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hoursFocal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours; EEG may be considered, and imaging only with abnormal or focal examination findingsThe seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes
Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't missNeonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningealProlonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes; red cells may be presentNot excluded; the same tap tests for it, and acyclovir is given until it is excluded
Meningococcemia Can't missN. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensationPetechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tapSkin examination normal, normotensive
Abusive head trauma Can't missInfant with subdural collectionsSeizure with a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages, with increased irritabilityNot excluded by the stated findings
Decision spine How old? – Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is ruled out · Is she seizing now? – No, it stopped in 4 minutes → no benzodiazepine · Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? – No → no EEG (electroencephalography) · Any sign of intracranial infection? – Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes · Does she need a CT first? – The fontanelle is open → no, so perform the lumbar puncture
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Age, exam and time to return to baselineFirstAge 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline within 10 minutesSimple febrile seizure: no tests needed
Lumbar punctureBy branchCSF pleocytosis; lymphocytes, and red cells may be present, in herpes simplex encephalitisMeningitis or encephalitis; tap for age under 6 months, full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness
Serum electrolytes and glucoseBy branchLow sodium or glucoseProvoked seizure; order with vomiting or diarrhea
Head CT or magnetic resonance imagingBy branchSubdural blood, a mass or edemaFocal signs, or papilledema with a closed fontanelle; infant with retinal hemorrhages
EEGBy branchFocal or epileptiform dischargesMay be considered for a complex febrile seizure, meaning one that is focal, over 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsNo test confirms a simple febrile seizureTests are for red flags, to exclude infection and other causes
Head CT before lumbar puncture, open fontanelleSkipThe open fontanelle decompresses the pressureTap without a CT first
Scenario bank
  1. 12-month-old girl with fever and a seizure who has papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit, with a closed anterior fontanelle → Antibiotics, then head CT, then lumbar puncture → The imaging exception
  2. 2-year-old with fever, seizure and persistently altered mental status whose cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells → Herpes simplex encephalitis → Add acyclovir to empiric therapy
  3. 18-month-old boy with temperature 39.1 C and a single 3-minute generalized seizure who is alert with a normal examination 20 minutes later → Reassurance and discharge → Simple febrile seizure
  4. 2-year-old girl with fever who is still convulsing 8 minutes after the seizure began → Intravenous lorazepam → Duration gates the benzodiazepine
  5. 3-year-old boy with fever, a generalized seizure, a spreading petechial rash and hypotension → Give empiric intravenous antibiotics immediately and perform the lumbar puncture afterward → Meningococcemia
  6. 6-week-old boy, afebrile, with a seizure, a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy → Neuroimaging → Abusive head trauma
  7. 4-year-old boy, now postictal after his third seizure of this febrile illness, this one left-sided and lasting 20 minutes → Electroencephalography → Complex febrile seizure (focal, 20 minutes, recurrent); EEG may be considered when a febrile seizure is focal or recurrent; he is no longer seizing, so no lorazepam, and a complex seizure warrants more than reassurance
  8. 10-week-old girl with fever, vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsiness persisting an hour later, an open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck and decreased tone → Lumbar puncture → Age outside the window plus signs of intracranial infection
  9. Why an open anterior fontanelle removes the usual requirement for head CT before lumbar puncture → It acts as a pop-off valve that decompresses rising intracranial pressure, limiting herniation risk → The anatomy suspends the rule
  10. Infant with fever, petechiae and hypotension in whom the lumbar puncture will be delayed; which action is inappropriate → Delaying antibiotics until the lumbar puncture is completed → Treat first, tap after
  11. 2 yo M, 2 days of rhinorrhea, fever 39.2 C this morning, a 3-minute generalized seizure, sleepy and confused when paramedics arrived, now alert and playful with a normal examination; uncle has epilepsy; immunizations current → Reassurance and discharge home → simple febrile seizure; the postictal drowsiness has resolved and an uncle's epilepsy changes nothing
  12. Parents of a 2 yo after a first simple febrile seizure ask what to expect → About 30% have another; epilepsy risk stays about 1 to 2% → antipyretics do not prevent the next one
  13. 2 yo back to baseline after a brief generalized febrile seizure, but with 2 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhea and dry mucous membranes → Serum electrolytes and glucose → hypoglycemia or hyponatremia can provoke a seizure
  14. 11-month-old boy after a first seizure, 2 minutes and generalized, at home. Temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 150/min. Now alert and playful; examination normal. He has received no pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine doses → Lumbar puncture → incomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap; maintenance antiseizure drugs are usually not indicated; EEG is not recommended after an initial simple febrile seizure with a normal neurologic examination
Decoy note A supple neck excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants. The criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. The rest of the examination is normal: tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin. With no source found, this strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it. When every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. Up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list but leave the four indications already present.
Counseling, and what each test is for Recurrence – about 30% have another febrile seizure · Epilepsy – risk slightly raised, about 1 to 2% · Antipyretics – treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure · Course – resolves by school age, with no effect on development · Risk factors – fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunization, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy · Timing – usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear · Brain imaging – focal neurologic signs · EEG – recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure · Admission – not back to neurologic baseline · Electrolytes and glucose – vomiting or diarrhea, since hypoglycemia and hyponatremia can provoke a seizure · Lumbar puncture – also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunization, or when already on antibiotics
Pearls Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, needs a lumbar puncture. An open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years. It is the fastest disqualifier, so check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, so infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child. The CT-before-tap rule therefore generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication. Then ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants may lack neck signs; read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead. A supple neck excludes nothing under 12 months. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is altered mental status, not a long febrile seizure, and it indicates a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension, reverse the order: antibiotics first, tap after. A sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable price.
Pairs with Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the workup when there is no seizure, up to the decision to tap. This brief covers what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Ask: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
Transferable rule For a benign diagnosis defined by an age range, check the age before weighing the findings, because age disqualifies it first. When a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent. If the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply.
True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging: The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary
Mirror twinReassurance and discharge: Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it
Salient decoyElectroencephalography: EEG may be considered for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam: Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing
