Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth

birth weight rules · four developmental laws · milestones at 2, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months · delay by domainDo the weight and milestones fit the age, and if not, which domain is delayed?

The decision point

Birth weight is regained by 10–14 days, doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 1 year and quadruples by 2 years. When the numbers match a milestone rule and the exam is normal, management is reassurance; any other intervention is unnecessary.

The four developmental laws
  • Motor descends the body – 2 mo lifts head · 4 mo head steady + forearms · 6 mo rolls / props on hands · 9 mo sits alone · 12 mo pulls to stand and cruises
  • Grasp moves pinky-side → thumb-side – 4 mo midline · 6 mo whole-hand reach · 9 mo raking · 12 mo pincer
  • Language: vowels → consonants → meaning – 4 mo "ooo" · 6 mo raspberries/squeals · 9 mo "mamama" · 12 mo "mama" meaning mama
  • Social: everyone → someone – 2 mo social smile at anyone · 6 mo familiar faces · 9 mo stranger and separation anxiety · 12 mo social games, object permanence
Age anchors
AgeImageHook
2 moThe Greeter – lifts head, tracks you, smiles, coosTWO eyes track, TWO lips smile
4 moThe Sphinx – head steady on forearms, hands to midline and mouthFOUR = everything to the FORE
6 moThe Roller – rolls, sits propped, mouths toys, laughsSIX: Sits, Squeals, raSpberries
9 moThe Anxious Sitter – sits alone, rakes, babbles, cries at strangersNINE = "No! Not you!"
12 moThe Little Person – cruises, pinches a Cheerio, first wordONE year = ONE word, ONE-finger pinch
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, birth weight 3.2 kg, now 6.6 kg, normal exam → Normal growth – weight doubles by 4 to 6 months → reassurance
  2. 10 day M who has not yet regained his birth weight → Normal weight loss – birth weight is regained by 10 to 14 days → reassurance
  3. 2 mo M who lifts his head and smiles socially → Age-appropriate development
  4. 9 mo M who cannot sit without support → Gross motor delay → developmental evaluation
  5. 6 mo M who does not babble and does not respond to sound → Audiology evaluation
  6. 12 mo M whose weight has tripled since birth → Normal growth → reassurance
  7. 18-month-old with a 12 to 15 word vocabulary understood mainly by family, frequent jargon, single words without phrases, who scribbles, follows a one-step command without gesture and shows stranger anxiety, but pulls to stand and only cruises → Gross motor delay → walking easily is expected by 18 months
  8. 18-month-old with isolated gross motor delay and otherwise normal development → Refer for early intervention services → under age 3 the referral is the pathway
  9. Why an 18-month-old’s language is normal although strangers understand few of his words → Speech is expected to be intelligible mainly to family at this age, with jargon normal → intelligibility milestones come later
  10. 4-year-old boy at a well-child visit who imitates a straight line but cannot copy a circle, jumps but cannot balance on one foot, and combines words with only half his speech understood; normal examination → Delayed gross motor, fine motor and language → global developmental delay: evaluate for a cause and refer to the school district for a preschool special education evaluation (early intervention is for children under 3)
  11. 4-year-old girl who hops on one foot, copies a square, draws a stick figure and plays cooperatively, but speaks in two-word phrases that strangers rarely understand → Isolated language delay → one delayed domain; obtain a hearing evaluation
  12. 4-year-old boy who speaks in sentences strangers understand and plays cooperatively with friends, but cannot hop on one foot and cannot copy a circle → Global developmental delay → two domains delayed: gross motor and fine motor
Red flags No social smile by 3 mo · no babbling by 9 mo · no words by 15 mo · not walking by 18 mo · hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiparesis) · loss of any acquired milestone at any age; regression is always pathologic (Rett, autistic regression, metabolic disease, leukodystrophy).
Primitive reflexes must leave before the skill arrives Palmar grasp gone 3–6 mo (enables voluntary grasp) · Moro by 6 mo · rooting by 4 mo · ATNR (asymmetric tonic neck reflex) by 4–6 mo · parachute appears 6–8 mo and stays for life · Babinski normal until 12–24 mo. Persistence beyond these windows indicates a UMN (upper motor neuron) lesion or cerebral palsy. Note: the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) 2022 revision moved milestones from the 50th to the 75th percentile. As a result, "sits without support" is now listed at 9 months, where older sources say 6.
The 18-month set, and the ages that neighbour it Walks easily and climbs – the gross motor item · Scribbles – fine motor · At least 3 words beyond mama and dada, with frequent jargon – language; intelligibility to strangers is not expected yet · Follows a one-step command without gesture – cognitive · Two-word phrases belong to 24 months and 75% intelligible speech to age 3; neither is expected at 18 months · Stranger anxiety is normal from 6 to 9 months to about age 2 and supports intact social development
The 4-year set, and global delay Hops on one foot and throws a ball overhand – gross motor · Copies a square and draws a simple stick figure – fine motor · Speaks in sentences that strangers understand and tells stories – language · Plays cooperatively with friends – social · Jumping, imitating a line and combining words – younger skills; having them does not make a 4-year-old normal in that domain · Global developmental delay – significant delay in two or more domains; evaluate for a cause; under age 3, refer for early intervention; from age 3, refer to the school district for a preschool special education evaluation, with speech, physical and occupational therapy. How NBME framed it: the stem gives one skill present and one missing in each domain, and the options grid normal or delayed across three domains.
Pairs with Part I Feeding an Infant or Toddler covers the case where growth falters because of how the child eats rather than how much.
Salient decoyNormal in all three domains: jumping and combining words are skills of a 2-year-old, so having them does not make a 4-year-old normal
Unchecked attributeGross motor marked normal: he can jump, but a 4-year-old hops on one foot and this boy cannot balance on one
Unchecked attributeFine motor marked normal: imitating a line is not copying a shape; a 4-year-old copies a square, and this boy cannot copy a circle
Unchecked attributeLanguage marked normal: he combines words, but only half his speech is understood; a 4-year-old speaks in sentences strangers understand

Hypertension in an Adult

baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates themIs there end-organ injury or a comorbidity that picks the drug, and is the patient resistant, young or hypokalemic?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Confirmed hypertension gets one baseline panel: it looks for end-organ injury and the comorbidity that picks the drug.

  • End-organ injury, such as LVH (left ventricular hypertrophy) on ECG (electrocardiogram): start treatment at that visit; echo or stress testing never delays it.
  • No comorbidity: an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), thiazide or dihydropyridine CCB (calcium channel blocker), interchangeable first-line.
  • A comorbidity: match the drug to it. Gout takes losartan (mildly uricosuric); thiazides are avoided because they raise urate.
  • Resistant, young or hypokalemic: hunt a secondary cause. In a young patient, hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and normal renal function is mineralocorticoid excess.
  • Renin separates the look-alikes: suppressed in primary hyperaldosteronism, high in renal artery stenosis.
Diagnosis
Secondary hypertension: what to test for
DiagnosisThe stem showsFirst testConfirms, then
Primary hyperaldosteronismHypokalemia and alkalosisAldosterone-to-renin ratioAldosterone fails to suppress with salt loading; then adrenal CT (computed tomography) and adrenal venous sampling to lateralize
Fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, media of the artery)Young woman, abdominal bruitRenal artery duplex or CT angiographyCT or MR (magnetic resonance) angiography; catheter angiography is the reference standard
PheochromocytomaEpisodic hypertension, headache, sweatingPlasma or urine metanephrinesMetanephrines several-fold high; then adrenal CT or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to locate the tumor
Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, obesity, daytime sleepinessPolysomnographyPolysomnography is itself confirmatory; a home study can screen
Coarctation of the aortaWeak femoral pulses, rib notchingEcho or CTArm-leg pressure gradient first at the bedside; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing
Cushing syndromeStriae, moon facies, hyperglycemiaLow-dose dexamethasone or 24-hour cortisolA second, different screening test abnormal (late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urine cortisol, 1 mg dexamethasone); then ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) to localize
Mechanism Aldosterone – raises ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) in the collecting duct; sodium reabsorption leaves the lumen electronegative, which drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion: hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis · Aldosterone escape – through ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) and pressure natriuresis, sodium plateaus and there is no edema; a normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – classically flash pulmonary edema with severe hypertension in an elderly patient with vascular disease
Management and treatment
Antihypertensive choice by comorbidity
ComorbidityPreferred agents
Coronary diseaseAngina: β-blocker, CCB; after myocardial infarction: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus β-blocker
Heart failure with reduced ejection fractionACE inhibitor or ARB, β-blocker, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Atrial fibrillation or flutterβ-blocker, nondihydropyridine CCB
Chronic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB
GoutLosartan, other ARB, CCB; avoid diuretics
OsteoporosisThiazide diuretic
Migraineβ-blocker, CCB
Calcium kidney stonesThiazide diuretic
By situation Two drugs – stage 2 hypertension (BP 140/90 mm Hg or more): most adults start two first-line drugs from different classes, preferably as one single-pill combination · LVH – regresses on an ARB or ACE inhibitor · Atrial fibrillation – a β-blocker or a nondihydropyridine CCB controls rate and treats the pressure; avoid combining them (bradycardia, heart block, depressed contractility) · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – when severe, an ACE inhibitor can cause AKI (acute kidney injury): the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR (glomerular filtration rate)
Practice
  1. 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL → Losartan → gout picks losartan, which is mildly uricosuric; a thiazide raises urate, and stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the hypertrophy and invites a flare
  2. 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium loss, so one drug treats both the pressure and the osteoporosis; losartan and a dihydropyridine CCB treat only the pressure
  3. 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L → ACE inhibitor → albuminuric chronic kidney disease takes an ACE inhibitor or ARB; a thiazide or a nondihydropyridine CCB treats only the pressure
  4. 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min → Beta-blocker → a beta-blocker treats both the pressure and the migraine, one drug for both diagnoses; a thiazide treats only the pressure, and hydralazine is not a first-line class
  5. 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium and treats both; a loop diuretic increases urinary calcium, and losartan treats only the pressure
  6. 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Start an antihypertensive now → left ventricular hypertrophy is end-organ injury, the treatment gate; echo or stress testing only characterizes it and never delays the first drug
  7. 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Aldosterone-to-renin ratio → hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function are mineralocorticoid excess; a suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease, and a normal sodium (aldosterone escape) does not argue against it. Duplex fits a bruit, metanephrines fit spells
  8. 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Fibromuscular dysplasia → a young woman with an abdominal bruit and high renin has fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, a disease of the media): CT angiography. Primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; coarctation weakens the femoral pulses
  9. 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min → Pheochromocytoma → episodic hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating is pheochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines, several-fold high, then adrenal CT or MRI. A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone argues against hyperthyroidism, and panic disorder is not diagnosed when another condition better explains the spells
  10. 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg → Coarctation of the aorta → weak femoral pulses, rib notching and an arm-leg pressure gradient are coarctation of the aorta; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing. Renal artery stenosis does not explain weak femoral pulses, rib notching or an arm-leg gradient, and pheochromocytoma commonly brings episodic headaches, sweating and a racing heart, and he has neither sweating nor palpitations
  11. 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L → Obstructive sleep apnea → snoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity with resistant hypertension are obstructive sleep apnea: polysomnography, itself the confirmatory test. Snoring, sleepiness and a thick neck point to the airway first, and there are no striae to suggest Cushing syndrome
  12. 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL → Cushing syndrome → striae, moon facies and hyperglycemia are Cushing syndrome: an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, then a second, different screening test, then ACTH to localize
  13. 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed → Adrenal venous sampling → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is more common than adenoma, so adrenal venous sampling lateralizes before any adrenalectomy; another CT shows the anatomy again, not which gland secretes
  14. 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL → An ACE inhibitor → the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR, so with bilateral lesions an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated: it can cause AKI; a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide are effective at controlling pressure in renal artery stenosis
  15. 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL → Angiotensin II → renin initiates the cascade and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia, but angiotensin II directly mediates the vasoconstriction
Common wrong answers Discontinue the allopurinol: the uric acid level baits it, but it lowers nothing that matters; it treats neither the pressure nor the LVH and invites a flare. Echo or stress testing first: characterization never delays treatment.
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: fibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient. Part II Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child: low potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status.
Transferable rule

Store the pairings, never a favorite drug: the same agent is preferred with one comorbidity and avoided with another. Name what the evidence proves: labs prove the physiology (hyperaldosteronism), imaging or pathology proves the lesion (adrenal adenoma).

Intimate Partner Violence

plan for safety, report by who is at riskIs she safe at home, and who decides what happens next?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Suspect IPV (intimate partner violence) when frequent injuries come with explanations that do not fit, and/or when bruises sit in a suspicious distribution: lower abdomen, back or forearms.

Ask her tactfully whether she feels safe at home, alone if possible.

Every patient gets help developing an emergency safety plan, whether or not she discloses abuse or is ready to leave.

Suspected abuse of a child in the home is reported on suspicion; reporting her own abuse varies by state and is not the first step.

Diagnosis
Raise it Injuries – frequent, with explanations that do not fit; forearms may bruise from defensive movements · Risk factors – recent job loss or job or financial instability; substance use · Pregnancy – IPV often begins or increases, especially in unintended pregnancy · No test – the injury pattern and the history raise it
Management and treatment
What every patient gets, then what depends on her answer
StepWho gets itWhy
See her aloneEvery patient, if possibleA partner present can intimidate her
Ask, tactfully and in a nonthreatening manner, whether she feels safeEvery patient with suspicious findingsAsking directly, in private, helps her disclose
Emergency safety planEvery patientMany are not yet willing or able to leave
Assess readiness to actShe says she is abusedShe decides when to leave
ReportSuspected child abuse, or state law requires itA legal duty; for her own abuse, it varies by state

If seeing her alone is not possible or not offered, the safety plan comes first.

The safety plan Include – a place to flee to if needed; signals or code words that tell her children or neighbors to call for help; an emergency kit stored outside the home · Avoid – generally, written materials such as pamphlets, because the abuser can find them · Resources – local shelter and national hotline information in a form safe to carry (wallet card, phone under a code name) · Every later visit – reassess her risk of immediate harm, privately
Who decides, and who must be reported
IfThen
Competent adult, not older or disabled (alert, oriented, judgment intact)She decides what to do and when; reporting her own abuse varies by state, and most states do not require it
Not yet willing and able to leave safelyPolice or a protective order may escalate harm
Prepared to actSupport the step she chooses
Only she is at riskSafety plan with her; no report as the first step
Suspected abuse of a child in the homeReport to child protective services on suspicion
Capacity impaired (older or dependent adult): she cannot decide for herselfReport per state law
An older or disabled adultMost states require a report
Injury from a gun, knife or other weaponReportable in most states
Where the state requires a report for herReport, but not as the first step

Most states require reports of specified injuries and wounds, and very few require reporting domestic violence itself; know your state's law.

Screening and complications Screen – the USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) recommends screening women of reproductive age for IPV, including during pregnancy and after delivery (grade B); screening often uses a brief questionnaire, asked in a private and safe setting · Positive screen – evaluate and, if appropriate, offer or refer for evidence-based interventions with several components and ongoing support · Complications – repeated injury, seen as frequent emergency visits; in pregnancy, miscarriage, preterm labor and low birth weight
Practice
  1. 31-year-old woman in the emergency department husband slapped and shoved her 2 hours ago wants to go home No psychiatric history HR 96/min · arm and back bruises · slightly disheveled, tearful, anxious · denies suicidal, homicidal ideation · alert, oriented; judgment intact → Develop an emergency safety plan with her → the danger is her home, not a psychiatric condition: judgment intact and no suicidal ideation; a competent adult decides when to leave
  2. 28-year-old woman in the emergency department cut lip; bruises on lower abdomen and back says she fell down the stairs 1 day ago her boyfriend stays and answers most questions T 37.0 °C · HR 98/min · alert, oriented; anxious → Interview her alone about her safety at home → the boyfriend answers for her, so see her alone first, if possible, to prevent intimidation; the safety plan every patient receives follows
  3. 34-year-old woman seen alone for a 2-day-old wrist sprain husband shoved and slapped her several times this year will not leave him: she has no income bruises on both forearms · HR 84/min · alert, oriented; thought process linear; judgment intact → Build an emergency safety plan with her → a competent adult not yet ready to leave; the plan protects her until she is, and therapy for perpetrators has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk of violence
  4. 35-year-old woman returns alone for a blood pressure check 1 month ago she said her husband hits her made a safety plan then BP 128/82 mm Hg · HR 76/min · no new injuries · alert, oriented, euthymic → Ask again, privately, about her current safety → assess the risk of immediate harm at every visit
  5. 32-year-old woman seen alone at a clinic her husband hits her last week he struck their 6-year-old son with a belt, leaving welts she does not want to leave bruise on her upper arm · HR 80/min · alert, oriented, judgment intact → Report the child's abuse to child protective services → suspected child abuse is reported on suspicion; her own safety plan continues, and reporting her own abuse follows state law
  6. 81-year-old woman with dementia, brought by her husband, her caregiver bruises on both upper arms he says she falls; her gait is steady HR 78/min · oriented to person only; cannot name the year · poor insight and judgment → Report the abuse to Adult Protective Services → she cannot decide for herself, so seeing her alone cannot yield a plan she can carry out; most states require reporting the abuse of older adults, and waiting for a follow-up visit leaves her with the suspected abuser
  7. 27-year-old woman in the emergency department says her husband beats her plans to go home tonight is making a safety plan with the physician bruises on both forearms · HR 88/min · alert, oriented, judgment intact → A printed pamphlet to keep at home → written materials should generally be avoided, because the abuser may find them
  8. 23-year-old woman, 20 weeks, unplanned pregnancy lower-abdominal bruises; says she walked into a table second injury visit in 2 months partner answers for her No alcohol or drug use HR 88/min · platelets 250,000/mm³ · fetal heart rate 145/min · alert, oriented, anxious → Intimate partner violence → lower-abdominal bruises, a story that does not fit and a partner who speaks for her; IPV often begins or increases in pregnancy, especially unintended
  9. 30-year-old woman in the emergency department swollen, tender forearms with bruises along both 1 day after what she calls a trip over a rug third injury visit this year HR 92/min · BP 124/80 mm Hg · alert, oriented; anxious → Raising the arms to shield the face and torso → the forearms may bruise from defensive movements during an attack
  10. 29-year-old woman seen alone in the emergency department bruised cheek; her boyfriend punched her last night asks that the police not be told No children HR 90/min · alert, oriented, calm; judgment intact → Plan for her safety and respect her refusal → a competent adult: reporting her abuse varies by state and most states do not require it; where required, it is still not the first step; Adult Protective Services is for older or dependent adults
  11. 24-year-old woman at a routine health maintenance visit no complaints; came alone takes an oral contraceptive Never screened for partner violence HR 72/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · no injuries · alert, oriented, euthymic → A private brief questionnaire on partner violence → the USPSTF recommends screening women of reproductive age (grade B); screening often uses a brief questionnaire, asked in a private and safe setting
How NBME framed it: question 1

26-year-old woman in the emergency department with a broken arm she attributes to a fall third emergency visit in 6 months: earlier a broken ankle and a concussion apologizes and calls herself clumsy Left teaching after her third child's birth 8 months ago; lost income, significant financial strain; husband works two jobs No psychiatric illness or significant medical history alert, slightly disheveled, mildly anxious; often glances at her husband before answering vital signs normal · swollen right forearm · several bruises on upper extremities and stomach, from often bumping into things, she says

Most appropriate first course of action?

Competing answers
  • Admit to an inpatient psychiatric facility: she is in danger; but from her home situation, not a psychiatric condition; admission removes her only for a while.
  • Contact the police: the injuries are serious; some states may require it, but it is not the first step; before she is willing and able to leave safely, it may escalate the violence.
  • Recommend anger management therapy for her husband: he is the source; but therapy has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk of violence.
  • Recommend an order of protection against her husband: it sounds protective; but filed before she is willing and able to leave safely, it may increase the risk of harm.

Down to two: a safety plan or contacting the police. Safety plan: all patients with suspected abuse get help with one, whether or not they disclose abuse. The stem never says abuse: repeated injuries, an apologetic story that does not match the bruises, and a patient who looks at her husband before answering; four options act through the police, the courts, a psychiatric unit or the husband, and only the safety plan acts with her.

Pairs with Elder Abuse: the older adult who cannot protect herself, where suspicion alone leads to a report. Ask: can the injured adult decide for herself? Suspected Child Abuse: the injured child. Ask: is the person being harmed a child?
Transferable rule

When a competent adult is being hurt at home, the first action is one she can use today: ask her alone, then build a safety plan with her, whatever she discloses. Reporting follows who is at risk and state law, and it is not the first step for her own abuse.

Kawasaki Disease

CRASH and Burn criteria · incomplete disease · IVIG and aspirin within 10 days · echocardiogram · coronary complicationsHas fever lasted 5 days with 4 criteria, and is the child still inside the 10-day window?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

Diagnosis is clinical: fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) must be given within 10 days of fever onset, with aspirin, and an echocardiogram is obtained at diagnosis. Treat now; do not delay it for a workup. Sterile pyuria is a feature of Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease causes urethritis, giving urinary white blood cells with no bacteria.

Exception: with only 2 or 3 criteria (incomplete disease, especially in infants under 6 months), use CRP (C-reactive protein) and ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), supplemental labs and echocardiography, and treat if they are supportive.

Illness script
Kawasaki disease
What it isMedium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries
DriverImmune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown
TriggersNone proven; age under 5 and Asian ancestry, especially Japanese, raise risk (non-modifiable)
WhoYoung children; infants under 6 months have the most atypical presentations
LooksFever for 5 days or more with the CRASH findings; irritable
LabsAnemia, low albumin, high ALT (alanine aminotransferase), sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7
CourseUntreated, coronary aneurysm risk is ~20–25%; IVIG within 10 days lowers it to ~3–5%
Chain: Kawasaki disease

Vasculitis

→ an immune response inflames medium-sized arteries

→ the coronary arteries are the main target

Structural

→ the inflamed coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm

→ the aneurysm can expand, rupture or clot

Clinical

→ myocardial ischemia or infarction

→ heart failure: fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure, big heart

How it hides in a stem
History and examination: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Fever for 5 days or moreBurn: the gate; then count the criteria
"Pink eye"Nonexudative conjunctivitis: a criterion; pus points to adenovirus
Strawberry tongue, cracked red lipsOral criterion; ulcers point to Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Red swollen hands; later, peeling at the nailsExtremity criterion; the peeling comes in week 2 to 3
A single neck node 1.5 cm or largerAdenopathy, the least common criterion
Past high fever, red eyes, swollen red hands, big nodes, cracked lipsAn earlier Kawasaki illness: fever plus 4 criteria
That illness cleared on its own within 14 daysUntreated: no IVIG, so the coronary risk remained
The illness was 2 months beforeTime for aneurysms to cause heart failure ⚠︎ (role inferred)
A boy of 18 monthsThe usual age: most cases are under 5 ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Brought to the emergency department; 2 days of increasingly rapid breathing, irritableAn acute presentation; the symptom asked about: heart or lung? ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Now in obvious discomfortAn ill child; fits low cardiac output ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Vital signs, tests and pertinent negatives: what each clue points to
ClueWhat it points to
Temperature 38 C (100.4 F) two months laterLow grade: an ill child, not a new Kawasaki fever ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Pulse 150/min, respirations 60/minTachycardia, tachypnea: heart failure; tamponade shares them ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Blood pressure 60/40 mm HgHypotension: low output; tamponade also lowers it ⚠︎ (role inferred)
No other abnormal finding on examinationNo murmur: argues against mitral obstruction; no jugular distension or pulsus paradoxus argues against tamponade
Cardiomegaly on the chest x-rayA big heart; interstitial lung disease would show fibrosis
ST-segment depression in leads II and IIIIschemia from coronary disease ⚠︎ (role inferred)
Left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviationVentricular strain in a failing heart ⚠︎ (role inferred)
White cells in the urine, no bacteriaSterile pyuria: part of Kawasaki disease, not a UTI (urinary tract infection)
Weeks after COVID-19, vomiting, low blood pressureMIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children), not Kawasaki disease
Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria Kawasaki disease – fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria · Incomplete disease – fever for 5 days or more with only 2–3 criteria · Evaluate for incomplete disease – an infant 6 months or younger with fever for 7 days or more and no other explanation · IVIG resistance – fever persisting 36 h after IVIG
CRASH and Burn
  • Conjunctivitis – bilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing
  • Rash – polymorphous, perineal accentuation with desquamation
  • Adenopathy – cervical ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral (the least common criterion)
  • Strawberry tongue / cracked red lips – no ulcers, no exudate
  • Hands and feet – erythema and edema acutely, periungual desquamation in week 2–3
  • Burn – fever ≥5 days
First tests
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CRP and ESRFirstElevatedSupports Kawasaki
EchocardiogramFirstCoronary dilation or aneurysmBaseline at diagnosis; in suspected incomplete disease, coronary changes justify IVIG
CBC (complete blood count), albumin, ALT and urinalysisBy branchAnemia, low albumin, high ALT, sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7Supportive labs for incomplete Kawasaki; in incomplete disease, a raised CRP or ESR triggers supplemental labs and echo
Rapid strep testBy branchPositive, with sandpaper rash and no conjunctivitisScarlet fever: penicillin
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsFever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 criteriaTests support and stage it; IVIG within 10 days is not delayed for them
Urine culture for the pyuriaSkipSterile pyuria is part of KawasakiUrethritis from the disease; do not hold IVIG for a UTI workup
Kawasaki mimics and their discriminators
DiagnosisThe stem showsDecides itConfirms
AdenovirusFever, red eyes, sore throatExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; Kawasaki's is nonexudativeViral testing of a throat or eye swab
Scarlet feverFever, strawberry tongue, responds to penicillinSandpaper rash, Pastia lines, no conjunctivitisRapid strep test; throat culture if negative
MeaslesCough/coryza, unvaccinatedKoplik spots, cephalocaudal rashMeasles antibody serology or viral testing
MIS-CPost-COVID, older children, prominent GI symptomsShockClinical criteria plus a positive COVID-19 test or antibodies
Toxic shock syndromeFever, rash, desquamation laterHypotension + multiorgan failureClinical criteria; negative cultures
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysisTarget lesions, drug exposureMucosal erosions and ulcersClinical; skin biopsy
Staphylococcal scalded skinPerioral crustingNikolsky positiveClinical
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
Diagnosis madeIVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin, within 10 days of fever onsetFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
Seen after day 10IVIG if unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESRFever persisting 36 h after IVIG
IVIG resistanceSecond IVIG dose; steroids or infliximab as alternativesTop rung

Step down: high-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose once afebrile for 48 to 72 hours (practice varies). Kawasaki is the exception to the rule against aspirin in children.

Follow-up and return precautions Echocardiogram – at diagnosis, then 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks after treatment in uncomplicated disease ⚠︎ (a 2024 guideline update may shorten the first recheck; unverified) · Return – fast breathing or irritability weeks later needs an ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiogram
Distractors
Salient decoyUrine culture and antibiotics: pyuria looks like a UTI; it is sterile and part of the disease.
Sequencing trapWaiting for a fourth criterion: coronary changes on the echocardiogram already justify IVIG.
Unchecked attributeNo IVIG after day 10: the 10-day mark is a target, not a cutoff; with persistent unexplained fever or coronary changes and a raised CRP or ESR, IVIG is still reasonable.
True-fact-wrong-slotAvoiding aspirin in a child: the Reye rule is real, but Kawasaki is the exception.
Prevention and screening
  • No vaccine or drug prevents Kawasaki disease; IVIG within 10 days prevents most aneurysms.
  • Live vaccines: MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella must be deferred 11 months after IVIG.
Complications and long-term sequelae
  • Coronary aneurysm: can expand, rupture or cause a myocardial infarction; infants under 6 months have the highest aneurysm risk.
  • Heart failure: tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, cardiomegaly and ischemic ST depression.
  • Pericardial effusion: a real complication; tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus.
  • Mitral valve: regurgitation, not stenosis.
  • Lungs and pulmonary vessels: rarely involved.
  • Workup: ECG and echocardiogram as soon as Kawasaki is suspected.
Practice
  1. 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL → IVIG now → give IVIG even beyond day 10 when unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESR
  2. 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation → Congestive heart failure → late cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki disease: cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression, and no murmur or signs of tamponade
  3. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm → Kawasaki disease → fever 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG plus aspirin
  4. 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation → IVIG and aspirin now → incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding
  5. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis → Scarlet fever → a positive rapid strep test confirms it; penicillin
  6. 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward → Measles → Koplik spots and a descending rash decide it; measles antibody serology confirms
  7. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria → Continue IVIG and aspirin as planned → sterile pyuria is Kawasaki urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis
  8. 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised → Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children → weeks after COVID-19, with prominent GI symptoms and shock
  9. 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands → Echocardiogram → baseline coronary assessment at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it
  10. 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ → Coronary artery aneurysm → echocardiogram now; untreated aneurysms can progress to infarction or heart failure
  11. 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist → Second dose of IVIG → fever persisting 36 h after IVIG defines resistance
  12. 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → live vaccines are deferred 11 months after IVIG; inactivated vaccines are not
  13. 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal → Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeks → coronary changes can appear after a normal first study
How NBME framed it The untreated Kawasaki illness sits in the past history as an episode that resolved on its own, and the mechanism lead-in is keyed to heart failure. The criteria appear in lay words ("pink eye," swollen hands) and are never named.
Distractors: NBME question
True-fact-wrong-slotPericardial effusion: a real Kawasaki complication, but tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression fits heart failure.
Unchecked attributeMitral valve obstruction: Kawasaki affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis, and no stenotic murmur is heard.
Salient decoyChronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease: Kawasaki rarely involves the lungs, and the film shows cardiomegaly rather than interstitial fibrosis.
Class-vs-memberThickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries and rarely involves the pulmonary vessels.
Pairs with Part I Heart Failure in a Child: is the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis?
Transferable rules

A candidate diagnosis that explains only a subset of the findings is wrong. A UTI (urinary tract infection) explains two of the findings; Kawasaki explains all of them. Check which findings a diagnosis leaves unexplained.

Lithium Therapy

which complication, and what to doIs this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Act first: in lithium toxicity, decreased consciousness, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia calls for hemodialysis at any level.

New symptoms on lithium: read three pairs together:

  • serum sodium with urine osmolality
  • lithium level with the neurologic examination
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) with free thyroxine

High sodium with dilute urine after years of lithium is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: replete volume, and stop lithium if possible.

Coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia or confusion with a raised level is toxicity (commonly above 1.5 mmol/L; lower in chronic toxicity): stop lithium and give IV isotonic fluids.

High TSH with low free thyroxine is hypothyroidism: add levothyroxine and continue lithium. A mildly high TSH with normal free thyroxine and no symptoms is the routine thyroid change.

Diagnosis
Which complication Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus – little or no response to desmopressin · Adverse effects – LMNOP (mnemonic below)
LMNOP
  • L – lithium
  • M – movement: tremor
  • N – nephrology: kidney injury and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (thirst and urination)
  • O – hypothyroidism
  • P – pregnancy: Ebstein's anomaly
Which one: the stem and the decider
ComplicationThe stem showsDecides it
Chronic lithium toxicityLong-term user; new thiazide, NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker); dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, low-sodium diet or kidney injuryLong-term use; neurologic findings lead: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion; raised level
Acute lithium toxicityRecent large ingestionLarge ingestion; nausea, vomiting, diarrhea often come first
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusYears of lithium; thirst, polyuria; confusion with dehydrationHigh sodium, dilute urine
HypothyroidismTiredness, cold intolerance, mental fogginess; may have a goiter; middle-aged women at highest riskHigh TSH, low free thyroxine
Routine side effectsFine tremor, polyuria, mildly high TSHSodium, mental status, free thyroxine normal
Management and treatment
Management ladder: lithium toxicity
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop lithium; IV isotonic fluids; serial levelsDecreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmia; level over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidneys
EscalationHemodialysisTop rung
By situation Mild toxicity – stopping lithium may be sufficient · Ingestion – activated charcoal does not bind lithium (it may be given for a suspected coingestion); gastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation may be considered, particularly for sustained-release tablets · Diabetes insipidus, drowsy and volume-depleted – replete volume and check the level; a thiazide can treat the disorder but raises the lithium level · Hypothyroidism – add levothyroxine; thyroid abnormalities are not a reason to stop lithium · Routine thyroid change – continue lithium; recheck TSH in 4 to 6 months · Return – infection, heavy sweating or diarrhea (a dose reduction should be considered), or any new interacting drug
Lithium monitoring
WhenCheck
Before startingCreatinine, BUN (blood urea nitrogen), TSH, calcium with albumin; weight, height, blood pressure
Cardiac risk or age 50 or olderAdd an ECG before starting
After startingLevel every 1 to 2 weeks until two in a row are in range at one dose
Every 6 to 12 monthsLevel, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, TSH
New ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or NSAIDLevel and creatinine more often
YearlyCalcium with albumin; PTH (parathyroid hormone) if calcium is high

Level target: a trough about 12 hours after the last dose; 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance (some sources use 0.8 as the lower bound).

Practice
  1. 59-year-old man with bipolar disorder, on lithium 8 years lisinopril started 2 weeks ago 4 days of nausea and a coarse tremor of both hands alert and oriented HR 64/min · BP 126/80 mm Hg · sodium 139 mEq/L → Serum lithium level and creatinine → an ACE inhibitor raises the lithium level; coarse tremor and nausea suggest toxicity
  2. 44-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable lithium 6 years 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea drowsy; oriented to person only coarse tremor, slurred speech, unsteady gait HR 56/min · sodium 138 mEq/L · creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) · urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg → Chronic lithium toxicity → dehydration raised the level in a long-term user, and neurologic findings lead; a serum lithium level confirms
  3. 22-year-old woman took 30 immediate-release lithium tablets 2 hours ago started lithium 3 weeks ago vomited 3 times; diarrhea alert, oriented; no tremor HR 96/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg · lithium 3.2 mmol/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → IV isotonic fluids and serial lithium levels → alert, kidneys working and level under 4.0 mmol/L: no dialysis criterion is met; lithium does not bind charcoal
  4. 67-year-old man on lithium for 15 years a week of poor intake; took extra tablets yesterday drowsy, confused; responds only to a loud voice coarse tremor HR 54/min · BP 100/62 mm Hg · lithium 4.4 mmol/L · creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.1) → Urgent hemodialysis → decreased consciousness, or a level over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidneys: either one indicates dialysis; lithium does not bind charcoal
  5. 62-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable lithium dose for 9 years hydrochlorothiazide started for hypertension 3 weeks ago now coarse tremor, slurred speech, confusion HR 60/min · lithium 2.4 mmol/L · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Increased renal reabsorption of lithium → a thiazide increases renal reabsorption of lithium, which is handled like sodium; the kidney is its only real exit
  6. 54-year-old man on lithium for 10 years for bipolar disorder knee osteoarthritis pain; asks what to take for it euthymic, alert and oriented BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Oral naproxen, taken daily → NSAIDs raise the lithium level
  7. 46-year-old man on lithium for 14 years 6 months of thirst passing large volumes of urine day and night euthymic, alert and oriented BP 124/78 mm Hg · sodium 146 mEq/L · glucose 94 mg/dL · urine osmolality 160 mOsm/kg → Collecting duct unresponsive to antidiuretic hormone → lithium blocks the ADH (antidiuretic hormone) signal, so fewer aquaporins reach the membrane; desmopressin changes the urine little or not at all
  8. 58-year-old woman on lithium for 16 years months of thirst and polyuria in bed 2 days after a fall now drowsy and disoriented HR 104/min · BP 102/64 mm Hg · sodium 156 mEq/L · urine osmolality 140 mOsm/kg · creatinine 1.3 mg/dL → IV fluid replacement and a serum lithium level → water and volume loss from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; dehydration also raises the lithium level
  9. 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 18 months 2 months of tiredness and feeling cold small nontender goiter alert and oriented HR 62/min · TSH 12.4 μU/mL · free thyroxine low · sodium 140 mEq/L · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Add levothyroxine and continue lithium → lithium-induced hypothyroidism; thyroid abnormalities are not a reason to stop lithium
  10. 26-year-old man, lithium for 4 months; euthymic mild tremor holding a cup urinating more than before alert, oriented, gait normal HR 72/min · sodium 140 mEq/L · urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg · TSH 5.6 μU/mL · free thyroxine normal · trough 0.9 mmol/L → Expected lithium adverse effects → normal sodium, mental status, level and free thyroxine; a fine tremor, polyuria and a mildly high TSH are routine
  11. 40-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 3 years takes no other medications routine visit; last laboratory studies 12 months ago alert and oriented BP 118/74 mm Hg · BMI (body mass index) 23 kg/m² → Lithium level, creatinine, TSH and calcium → level, electrolytes, creatinine and TSH every 6 to 12 months; calcium yearly
How NBME framed it: question 1

50-year-old woman brought to the emergency department: trouble speaking, cannot walk mildly agitated, uncooperative, not oriented to place Husband: lithium for 20 years for bipolar disorder; lately more thirst and urination No family history of kidney or endocrine disease 163 cm, 77 kg, BMI 29 kg/m² · T 36.8 °C · pulse 84/min · BP 110/75 mm Hg · speech difficulty, muscle weakness, the cognitive findings; otherwise normal · sodium 150 mEq/L · TSH 5.5 μU/mL · urine specific gravity 1.005 · urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg

Most likely cause of her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Acute lithium toxicity: confusion and trouble walking fit toxicity; but acute toxicity follows a large ingestion, and the labs here point to the kidney.
  • Lithium-induced hypothyroidism: the TSH of 5.5 is mildly high; but no free thyroxine is given, and hypothyroidism explains neither the hypernatremia nor the dilute urine.
  • Routine side effects of lithium: polyuria alone is routine; but dehydration, confusion, hypernatremia and dilute urine can be life-threatening.
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus: a BMI of 29 with polyuria suggests glucose diuresis; but hypernatremia after years of lithium fits the kidney better.

Down to two: lithium-induced diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. Diabetes insipidus: 20 years of lithium, thirst and polyuria, then a sodium of 150 with urine osmolality 200; the kidney is losing water it should keep. The stem never names diabetes insipidus or gives a lithium level, so the answer rests on reading the sodium against the urine. Four of the five options are lithium effects, and the one lab placed to tempt, a mildly high TSH, belongs to the wrong one.

Pairs with Polyuria: the renal workup of a dilute urine and the agent used when lithium must continue. Teratogenic Exposures: lithium in pregnancy. Thyroid Disease in an Adult: reading the TSH.
Transferable rule

When a patient on a drug with several known complications presents, choose the complication that explains every abnormal value. On lithium, a high sodium with dilute urine belongs to the kidney, and a mildly high TSH beside it is not the answer.
