Jaundice in a Newborn

timing, direct fraction and Coombs · the sick neonate with a positive screenIs the infant well, and is any of it direct?

WorkupCausesSick neonatePractice
Bottom line

Physiologic jaundice is a conjugation lag: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while hepatic uridine diphosphate (UDP) glucuronosyltransferase is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. A raised direct fraction makes newborn jaundice urgent.

  • Physiologic jaundice: begins after 24 hours, peaks around day 3 to 5, predominantly indirect, resolving by 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Pathologic jaundice: within the first 24 hours, any raised direct fraction, or persistence beyond 2 weeks.
  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice.
  • Classic galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency; galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the liver. Conjugated jaundice, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after milk feeds; it predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: indirect jaundice with anemia and Coombs-negative hemolysis, often after an oxidant.
Workup
Causes: timing and the direct fraction
Well or sick, indirect or direct
CauseWhenThe tell
PhysiologicAfter 24 hours, peak day 3 to 5Well infant, feeding and voiding normally; indirect; nothing but time
Suboptimal-intake (breast-feeding) jaundiceDay 3 to 5Weight loss, few wet diapers; feed more often, lactation support
Breast-milk jaundiceDay 7 onward, peak about 2 weeks, can persist weeksThriving, indirect, normal GGT and stools; continue breast-feeding
Blood group or Rh hemolytic diseaseOften within 24 hoursCoombs positive; mother group O or Rh-negative; high reticulocytes
G6PD deficiency Can't missVariable, can be abruptCoombs negative, anemia, high reticulocytes, often an oxidant; X-linked, mostly boys; Mediterranean, African or Asian ancestry; remove the trigger, phototherapy
Biliary atresia Can't missWell at birth; jaundice and hepatomegaly at 2 to 8 weeksDirect, high GGT and ALP, normal reticulocytes; acholic stools, dark urine; reducing substances negative
PFICInfancyDirect with a normal GGT; gallbladder present; specialist evaluation
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosisInfancy, acuteFebrile and ill; direct and GGT high, cytopenias, low reticulocytes, normal gallbladder; urgent hematology
Crigler-Najjar or GilbertPersistent indirectThe same enzyme absent or reduced, not immature; depends on type
Classic galactosemiaWithin days of milk feedsSick; conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly, urine reducing substances
Numbers and gates Visible – above about 5 mg/dL · Physiologic ceiling – peak around 14 to 15 mg/dL, indirect over 90% · Exchange range – generally above 20 mg/dL; kernicterus risk rises at 25 to 30 mg/dL · Under 24 hours – never physiologic: bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs · Any direct fraction – not physiologic: consider obstruction or infection · Beyond 2 weeks – check the direct fraction and the stool color before reassuring · Phototherapy versus exchange – phototherapy first; exchange for the severe range or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold · Feeding – almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding; more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
The sick neonate with a positive screen
Galactosemia: act now Stop – all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing · Feed – soy-based formula in place of breast milk and standard formula · In parallel – blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and empiric neonatal antibiotics for Escherichia coli · Confirm afterwards – red cell GALT activity · Urine test – needs recent intake, so a negative test after feeds stop does not exclude galactosemia
Screen-positive and sick: the liver and the urine name it
DiagnosisThe tell
Galactokinase deficiencyCataracts in a well infant; no liver disease, no sepsis
Congenital rubella syndromeCataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, blueberry muffin rash; present at birth, not triggered by milk
Hereditary fructose intoleranceAldolase B; same liver picture plus hypoglycemia, at weaning with fruit, juice or sucrose
Maple syrup urine diseaseEncephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis; sweet-smelling urine, ketosis
Practice
  1. 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery is jaundiced breast-feeding without difficulty; eight wet diapers daily alert; Apgar scores 10 and 10 Afebrile · total bilirubin 11 mg/dL → Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity → a well infant, feeding and voiding normally, jaundiced on day 4 at 11 mg/dL has physiologic jaundice: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while the conjugating enzyme is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. Enterohepatic circulation is increased in the newborn, not decreased, and ligandin is low at birth, not high: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction. Cholestasis would make the bilirubin direct, and albumin displacement needs a displacing drug
  2. 3-day-old girl born at term is seen at a follow-up visit newborn screen reported positive for galactosemia by telephone asymptomatic and breastfeeding well Afebrile · weight 3% below birth weight · no jaundice → Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation → presumptive galactosemia: stop all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing; replace breast milk with soy-based formula and confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. Continuing feeds continues the injury, and intravenous antibiotics answer a febrile or septic neonate, not this well one
  3. 4-week-old term boy, well-appearing, has weeks of yellowing of the eyes now jaundiced to the chest; exclusively breastfed stools fewer and paler; soft abdomen, enlarged liver ultrasound shows no visible gallbladder Afebrile · weight 25th percentile · total bilirubin 12.5 mg/dL → Direct bilirubin high, GGT high, reticulocyte count normal → pale stools and an absent gallbladder mean bile duct destruction, which raises the direct fraction and the GGT while the reticulocytes stay normal: biliary atresia. A direct rise with a normal GGT is progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and an indirect rise with high reticulocytes is hemolysis. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis also raises both, but in a febrile, ill infant with low reticulocytes. Exclusive breastfeeding suggests breast-milk jaundice, but that is indirect and leaves the stools yellow and the gallbladder normal. Intraoperative cholangiography confirms, then Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy
  4. 9-month-old girl has vomiting and jaundice began after juice and fruit were introduced liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · glucose 38 mg/dL → Hereditary fructose intolerance → aldolase B deficiency gives the same hepatic picture as galactosemia plus hypoglycemia, but it starts with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days; remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol. Glycogen storage disease type I brings hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with no dietary trigger; essential fructosuria is the benign cousin, a urinary sugar with no illness
  5. 2-day-old girl born at term has jaundice to the chest infant blood group B, mother group O direct Coombs test positive Alert and breast-feeding well Afebrile · total bilirubin 19 mg/dL · direct 0.6 mg/dL → Phototherapy → a positive Coombs test with a group O mother is isoimmune hemolysis, still below the exchange range. Phototherapy comes first; exchange transfusion is for the severe range (generally above 20 mg/dL) or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold. Jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
  6. 2-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia last week parents ask what she can be fed jaundice resolving on her current feeds Mother hopes to resume breastfeeding Afebrile · weight gain 25 g/day → Breast milk → breast milk and standard formula carry lactose, so they are replaced with soy-based formula; the diet reverses the acute illness. An elemental lactose-free formula carries no lactose either
  7. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed weight 11% below birth weight three wet diapers in the past day Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL, direct 0.4 mg/dL → Suboptimal-intake jaundice → weight loss and few wet diapers in the first week are a hungry infant: too little milk, not the milk itself, raising bilirubin through increased enterohepatic reabsorption (also called breast-feeding jaundice). Feed more often, with lactation support. Breast-milk jaundice is a thriving infant still jaundiced in the second week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction
  8. 10-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Newborn screen flagged a disorder of galactose metabolism Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Red cell GALT enzyme activity → red cell GALT activity names the enzyme defect: absent or near absent in classic galactosemia, and invalid after transfusion. Reduced red cell GALT activity establishes the diagnosis, so red cell enzyme analysis confirms it without hepatic tissue, and a serum galactose level only supports it
  9. 6-week-old girl born at term has jaundice acholic stools and dark urine liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin exclusively breast-fed; gaining weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 8 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Biliary atresia → a direct fraction is never physiologic, and acholic stools with dark urine at 2 to 8 weeks in an infant well at birth is duct obstruction. An exclusively breastfed infant can still have it: breast-milk jaundice is indirect, peaks around 2 weeks and leaves the stools yellow. Physiologic jaundice is predominantly indirect and resolves by 1 to 2 weeks
  10. 5-day-old boy born at term has poor feeding and lethargy seizures today urine smells like maple syrup Newborn screen reported positive T 36.9 °C · glucose 72 mg/dL · no hepatomegaly or jaundice → Leucine-free formula with dextrose → branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (signs from day 2 to 3) is encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, with sweet-smelling urine and ketosis: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error to confuse with galactosemia, but it carries ketoacids, not a reducing sugar. Soy formula, the galactosemia substitute, still contains protein, including the branched-chain amino acids, so it keeps feeding the block; protein is given as amino acids free of the branched chains, with isoleucine and valine added back, so the formula is leucine-free, and high calories come as dextrose and lipid. Antibiotics with observation do not lower plasma leucine
  11. 5-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the abdomen breast-feeding poorly with few wet diapers dry mucous membranes; weight 10% below birth weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 16 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Increased enterohepatic reabsorption → the newborn gut reabsorbs bilirubin, so anything that slows transit raises the indirect fraction: too little milk slows it and lets intestinal bilirubin return to the circulation. Conjugation is immature in every newborn, and albumin displacement requires a displacing drug
  12. 10-day-old girl born at term vomits after starting formula jaundiced, with the liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Classic galactosemia → conjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly, cataracts and urine reducing substances within days of milk feeds: liver, kidney, brain and lens are affected; eliminate galactose and lactose. Glycogen storage disease type I has no galactose trigger and no cataracts; hereditary fructose intolerance appears at weaning
  13. 14-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice of the face and chest breast-feeding well Uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · HR 140/min · transcutaneous bilirubin 9 mg/dL → Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs test → onset inside 24 hours is never physiologic, so it is pathologic until proven otherwise: send bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs test. Hepatic ultrasound and serum albumin cannot show hemolysis or immature conjugation
  14. 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia at 1 week bilateral cataracts seen on red reflex examination on soy formula; jaundice resolving Liver edge now 1 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · weight gain 30 g/day → Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase → cataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol, made by aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens: an osmotic lens injury. Galactokinase deficiency makes cataracts without ever forming galactose-1-phosphate, so the lens injury is galactitol, not galactose-1-phosphate; sorbitol is the diabetic product
  15. 4-day-old term boy of Greek descent is jaundiced to the abdomen feeding well Mother and infant both group A, Rh-positive direct Coombs negative; no spherocytes on smear hematocrit 36% · reticulocytes high · bilirubin 17 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL → G6PD enzyme activity level → Coombs-negative hemolysis (anemia with high reticulocytes) in a boy of Mediterranean ancestry is G6PD deficiency: X-linked, so mostly boys, and often an oxidant trigger. Osmotic fragility testing looks for spherocytosis, which the smear argues against, and a liver panel answers a raised direct fraction
  16. 8-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced vomits after breastfeeds liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances, dipstick glucose negative Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL → Stop breast milk and start soy-based formula → a conjugated fraction, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar after days of milk feeds indicate classic galactosemia: stop breast milk now and start soy formula. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise, and continuing feeds continues the injury; the diet reverses the liver disease, so transplant evaluation is not the step
  17. 3-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the chest a sulfonamide is proposed for a suspected urinary tract infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 15 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Displacement of bilirubin from albumin → free bilirubin crosses into the basal ganglia. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, so they are avoided in jaundiced newborns; when G6PD is deficient a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis, a second way it harms, excluded here by the normal enzyme. Glucuronosyltransferase activity sets how much bilirubin is conjugated and heme breakdown how much is made; the sulfonamide instead competes with bilirubin for albumin, raising the unbound fraction.
  18. 6-week-old boy born at term is well and growing bilateral cataracts on red reflex examination no hepatomegaly; no jaundice urine positive for reducing substances Passed newborn hearing screen; no murmur Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → Galactokinase deficiency → a block one step earlier diverts galactose to galactitol: cataracts in a well infant, with no liver disease and no sepsis; lactose-free diet. Classic galactosemia traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate and makes the whole sick-neonate picture; congenital rubella brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth and not triggered by milk
  19. 4-week-old boy born at term is well and feeding well jaundiced, with acholic stools urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · weight at the 40th percentile · total bilirubin 7 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan → a direct fraction in a well infant with acholic stools and negative reducing substances is biliary atresia: image first, then intraoperative cholangiogram confirms, and Kasai follows confirmation, before about 60 days. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise
  20. 3-day-old boy, formula-fed, has increasing lethargy and vomiting breathing rapidly; no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, clear lenses Urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · arterial pH 7.50, low carbon dioxide · ammonia markedly elevated · glucose 80 mg/dL → Urea cycle disorder → very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis in the first days of feeding, with no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts: hyperammonemia; stop protein and lower the ammonia. Classic galactosemia brings conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly and urine reducing sugar; maple syrup urine disease brings sweet-smelling urine and ketosis
  21. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed; weight 9% below birth weight only three wet diapers today; alert and well Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL · direct 0.4 mg/dL → Stopping breast-feeding → this is suboptimal intake, and jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: feed more often, not less, because milk intake drives bilirubin out through the gut. Lactation support with more frequent feeds, and phototherapy if the level crosses threshold, are both appropriate
  22. 3-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and doll-like facies massive hepatomegaly hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast No cataracts; urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · lactate 6 mmol/L · triglycerides 450 mg/dL · glucose 35 mg/dL → Glycogen storage disease type I → hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hypertriglyceridemia, with hypoglycemia within hours of fasting, no galactose trigger and no cataracts; treat with frequent cornstarch feeds. Galactosemia needs milk feeds and urine reducing sugar; hereditary fructose intolerance starts with fruit or sucrose at weaning
  23. 6-week-old boy born at term, jaundiced since 3 weeks of age clay-colored stools, dark urine ultrasound: small gallbladder, triangular cord sign intraoperative cholangiogram: no contrast reaches the duodenum Afebrile · direct bilirubin 6 mg/dL · GGT high → Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy → no contrast reaching the bowel confirms biliary atresia: Kasai before about 60 days, best done early, and most eventually need a liver transplant, so transplant is the later step, not the first. Ursodeoxycholic acid is given after the Kasai, not in place of it
  24. 12-day-old girl was diagnosed with galactosemia on day 6 on soy formula since diagnosis now lethargic and feeding poorly Jaundice improving; liver smaller T 38.8 °C · HR 186/min · capillary refill 3 seconds → Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicin → galactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a neonate with suspected sepsis gets a lumbar puncture once able to tolerate it: culture blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, then start empiric neonatal antibiotics. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so it is avoided in a jaundiced newborn, and observing off antibiotics leaves the infection untreated
  25. 3-week-old girl born at term is still jaundiced to the chest exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well yellow stools and pale urine Seen at a routine visit; examination otherwise normal Afebrile → Serum total and direct bilirubin → jaundice past 2 weeks needs a direct fraction, and the stool color, before reassurance; an indirect result in a thriving infant is breast-milk jaundice. A transcutaneous reading gives no direct fraction, and a Coombs test answers jaundice inside 24 hours, not prolonged jaundice
  26. 9-day-old breastfed girl has 3 days of vomiting and poor feeding jaundiced; liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts Normal hearing screen, no murmur; mother 39, declined vaccines T 38.4 °C · blood culture: Escherichia coli → Inability to metabolize galactose in breast milk → a milk-fed neonate with conjugated jaundice, a large liver, cataracts and Escherichia coli sepsis has classic galactosemia: stop breast milk and start soy formula without waiting for confirmation, and treat the sepsis in parallel. Congenital rubella, the vaccine decoy, brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth; a normal hearing screen and no murmur argue against it. Classic galactosemia is autosomal recessive, so the mother's age is a decoy
  27. 2-year-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia on newborn screening fed soy formula since day 5 parents ask about her long-term outlook Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile → Speech and learning problems and ovarian insufficiency can occur despite the diet → even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems (verbal dyspraxia), and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency. The diet reverses the acute liver, sepsis and cataract illness but does not prevent these, so normal fertility is not expected, and neither is progressive cirrhosis
  28. 3-week-old boy born at term is still jaundiced at a weight check exclusively breast-fed and gaining weight well yellow stools; thriving Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 13 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Breast-milk jaundice → milk beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin and increases enterohepatic circulation: from day 7, peaking around 2 weeks and able to persist for weeks, in a thriving infant with normal stools; continue breast-feeding. Suboptimal intake is a hungry infant losing weight in the first week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction and turns the stools pale
How NBME framed it: question 1

5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent with 2 days of progressive jaundice Five yellow, seedy stools a day; 2 ounces of cow's milk formula every 2 hours Born at term to a 32-year-old primigravida, who took an old sulfamethoxazole prescription for cystitis in the third trimester Mother and infant both group O, Rh-positive examination normal except jaundice from the head to the upper thighs hematocrit 33% · total bilirubin 20 mg/dL, direct 0.9 mg/dL direct and indirect Coombs tests negative

Most likely explanation for the jaundice?

Competing answers
  • Dehydration: raises indirect bilirubin through enterohepatic reabsorption; but feeds every 2 hours and five stools a day argue against it, and it does not cause anemia.
  • Sepsis: can raise indirect bilirubin; but he is well on examination, and Coombs-negative anemia after an oxidant exposure points to hemolysis.
  • Milk protein allergy: the cow's milk formula is the decoy; allergy causes reflux, enterocolitis, enteropathy or urticaria, not hemolysis.

Down to two: enzyme deficiency or physiologic jaundice. Enzyme deficiency: a total of 20 mg/dL exceeds the physiologic peak of about 15, and a hematocrit of 33% points to hemolysis. A negative Coombs removes isoimmune hemolysis; Mediterranean ancestry and a maternal sulfonamide point to G6PD deficiency. G6PD makes NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), which keeps glutathione reduced; without it, sulfonamides and other oxidants cause hemolysis. The key named only the class.

Read three labs together Direct high, GGT high, reticulocytes normal – duct obstruction: biliary atresia in a well infant with pale stools · Direct high, GGT normal – progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis · Direct and GGT high, reticulocytes low, cytopenias – hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a febrile, ill infant · Indirect, reticulocytes high – hemolysis · Indirect, everything else normal – breast-milk jaundice in a thriving infant; an exclusively breastfed infant can still have biliary atresia, so pale stools and a direct fraction decide it
The galactose pathway Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests. Galactokinase makes galactose-1-phosphate, and GALT converts it to uridine diphosphate galactose and glucose-1-phosphate. A galactokinase block leaves only galactitol, so cataracts alone; a GALT block traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate, so the whole sick-neonate picture, affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens. Cataracts in both come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens. Even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems, and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency.
Common wrong answers Ligandin or enterohepatic circulation: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction (ligandin is low and enterohepatic circulation increased in the newborn). Exchange transfusion at a level still in the phototherapy range. Maple syrup urine disease for a sick jaundiced neonate: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error, but no hepatomegaly, and ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar. Cystic fibrosis because the screen is positive: screened by immunoreactive trypsinogen, it presents with meconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with urinary sugar. Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidism: screen-positive with no hepatic picture; sickle cell jaundice is unconjugated and silent at 10 days because fetal hemoglobin protects. Urea cycle disorder: very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis, but no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts. Glycogen storage disease type I: hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with lactic acidosis, but no galactose trigger and no cataracts. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, and a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis when G6PD is deficient.
Exam answer versus current evidence Board questions use 60 days as the Kasai cutoff, and the Kasai is ideally done before 60 days. The evidence shows no sharp cutoff: native-liver survival falls continuously with age at operation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found operating at 30 days or earlier still better than at 31 to 60 days. Use 60 days as the exam threshold, not as a deadline with room to spare.
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Liver Tests: the conjugated-versus-unconjugated workup in adults. Hereditary fructose intolerance has no brief of its own: did symptoms start with fruit or sucrose? Biliary atresia: is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism: another positive newborn screen, where the thyroid-stimulating hormone level and the neck locate the defect; in galactosemia, the enzyme deficiency and the organism locate it.
Transferable rule

When every option names a real mechanism, check which direction each one moves in this patient before choosing. A positive newborn screen never names the disease when every disorder under consideration is on the panel: the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine identify it, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic diagnosis, not after it.

Tick-Borne Illness

treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triadWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, abdominal pain, body aches and headache with an unremarkable emergency department workup, now back with confusion and worse pain; lives by a lake surrounded by woods · Exam – T 39, BP 90/60, HR 120; new maculopapular rash on arms and legs, generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound, no neck stiffness, nonfocal neurologically · Labs – leukocytes 4,600, platelets 46,000, ALT (alanine aminotransferase) 158, AST (aspartate aminotransferase) 202, creatinine 1.1 · Imaging – abdominal CT (computed tomography) normal · Q – the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned amoxicillin, doxycycline, laparoscopy, prednisone, serum ceruloplasmin and stool ova and parasites
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt – 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of persistent fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area and is often bitten by mosquitoes; took corticosteroids for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill · Exam – T 39 C, HR 110, RR 22; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned dengue fever, erysipelas, erythema infectiosum, exanthema subitum, Kawasaki disease, measles, meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhoid fever
The decision point

The picture is three to four days of undifferentiated fever, headache and myalgia, then a rash on the extremities, in a child with wooded exposure. With the laboratory triad of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatremia, this is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The management is empiric doxycycline started now. Diagnosis is made retrospectively by serology, and the disease progresses to vascular collapse and death if you wait for it. The abdominal pain is not a second problem: severe abdominal pain is part of RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) in children. It is the specific reason this boy got a CT rather than an antibiotic on his first visit.

Defining criteria Rocky Mountain spotted fever – Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular organism transmitted by tick bite, peaking in late spring and summer, most often in the southeastern and south-central United States despite the name; incubation 2 to 14 days; many patients never recall the bite, so its absence proves nothing · The rash – begins maculopapular on the wrists and ankles, spreads centrally, involves palms and soles, and evolves to petechiae · The laboratory triad – thrombocytopenia from intravascular platelet destruction, hyponatremia, and raised AST and ALT from hepatic endothelial injury · Treatment gate – doxycycline empirically on suspicion, in all patients including young children; a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
Pertinent positives & negatives Three days of nonspecific fever then a rash – the rickettsial tempo; the rash appears late, which is why the first visit was unremarkable · Rash on arms and legs – extremity onset, spreading centrally · Platelets 46,000 with raised transaminases – the vascular-injury signature, belonging to no isolated abdominal process · Lives near woods – the exposure; no recalled bite is typical, not exculpatory · Severe abdominal pain with a normal CT – the pediatric RMSF mimic of appendicitis; the negative scan closes the surgical option rather than opening a new one · Confusion with a nonfocal examination and no neck stiffness – early encephalitic involvement, not meningitis · BP 90/60 with HR 120 – early vascular compromise, and the reason waiting is dangerous · No adenopathy, clear oropharynx – argues against the viral exanthems and mononucleosis
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure – the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Can't missSummer, wooded exposure; R. rickettsiiExtremity rash spreading centrally, palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases – (the answer)
Lyme diseaseSame season and habitat; Borrelia burgdorferiErythema migrans – a single expanding annular lesion with central clearingMaculopapular extremity rash; cytopenias and transaminitis atypical
Ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisSame tick exposure, similar prodromeSame labs, usually no rash; morulae in leukocytesA prominent rash is present
Dengue feverAedes mosquito; travel to or residence in the tropicsRetro-orbital pain, severe bone and muscle pain; leukopenia, low platelets; bleeding in severe casesNo tropical travel; mosquito bites at home in the US do not transmit it
MeningococcemiaNeisseria meningitidis; any seasonHours from fever to petechiae, purpura, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation; meningismus in someDays of fever before the rash; rash began distally and spread inward
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young childrenFever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5: nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, hand and foot redness or swelling, cervical node; platelets risePetechial palm rash, low platelets; conjunctival injection alone does not make it
MeaslesUnvaccinated child; paramyxovirusCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots; rash starts at the hairline and spreads down, sparing palms and solesRash began on the hands and wrists; no cough or coryza
Roseola (exanthema subitum)Human herpesvirus 6; under age 2Days of high fever in a well infant, then a blanching truncal rash as the fever breaksIll school-age child; petechial rash during the fever
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, otherwise well childIsolated thrombocytopenia, normal liver, afebrileFever, rash, transaminitis and hypotension
Wilson diseaseGenetic copper transport defectKayser-Fleischer rings; hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease over monthsAn acute febrile illness with a rash over days
AmebiasisFever, abdominal pain, liver abscessBloody diarrhea; abscess on imagingCT normal, no diarrhea, rash unexplained
Decision spine How long has the fever run and when did the rash appear? – Three to four days, then rash, the rickettsial tempo · Where did the rash start? – Wrists and ankles, spreading inward · What did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do? – Low, low, high, the triad · Any outdoor or wooded exposure? – Yes, and a recalled bite is not required · Is there abdominal pain? – In a child that is part of the disease, not a second one · So when do you treat? – Now; serology is retrospective and untreated disease kills
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Peripheral smearBy branchMorulae in leukocytes, usually no rashEhrlichiosis or anaplasmosis; doxycycline treats it too
Rickettsia rickettsii serology, acute and convalescentConfirmsFourfold rise in IgG titerRMSF, in retrospect; never delay treatment for it
Abdominal CTSkipNormalSevere abdominal pain is part of RMSF in children
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  3. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  4. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → a study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
  9. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → doxycycline now, without waiting for serology
  10. 10 yo F back 5 days from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic; fever 39.5 °C, retro-orbital headache, severe bone and muscle pain; macular truncal rash; no outdoor exposure in the US; white blood cell count 2,800/µL, platelets 90,000/µL → Dengue fever → supportive care with fluids; avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  11. 4 yo M on a Tennessee farm in July: 4 days of fever and headache; conjunctival injection; wrist and ankle macules, now petechial, spread to palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000/µL, sodium 130 mEq/L → Start doxycycline → Rocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion
Decoy note Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT is the classic pediatric RMSF presentation that gets children taken to the operating room. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Decoy note: no tick in the stem No tick – most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial · Mosquito bites – point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain · Conjunctival injection – occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down · Steroids for poison ivy a month ago – irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively – doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF – the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure – a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward – extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite – does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness – a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Part I Skin and Soft Tissue Infection covers the febrile-rash differential. Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and roseola, and Kawasaki Disease covers the 5-day fever with red eyes. Related conditions without their own brief: Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis. Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
How NBME framed it Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question.
Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands.
Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.

Brain Tumors in a Child

sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?

DiagnosisPracticeWorkup and management
Bottom line

Ask where the abnormal finding sits. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty with a normal neurologic examination points to the sella; ataxia or crossed findings point to the posterior fossa, where you localize side first and structure second. Image with MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); with papilledema, never tap first.

  • Suprasellar mass: classically a normal neurologic examination (no dysmetria, gait abnormality, focal weakness or skin findings); height crosses downward through percentiles while weight holds, with Tanner 1 past the pubertal gate and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrested puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed, and multiple axes point to the stalk, not the gland. Headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus make the mass midline and suprasellar.
  • Craniopharyngioma: from Rathke pouch remnants; cystic and calcified suprasellar mass: the cyst shows on MRI, the calcification mainly on CT; subtle for years before diagnosis.
  • Posterior fossa mass: 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumors but only 15 to 20% of adult ones, so in a child, ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
  • Hemisphere or vermis: limb dysmetria is hemispheric; a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared. Both together mean a hemispheric mass large enough to disturb midline structures; ipsilateral facial numbness fits (the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally), and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression.
  • Crossed findings: a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long-tract weakness on the other mean brainstem.
Diagnosis
Localizing signs Cerebellar signs – ipsilateral; the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion; face also ipsilateral; body long tracts contralateral · Hemisphere – limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline – truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus – direction-changing, gaze-evoked and unsuppressed; peripheral (vertigo) nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation · Raised-pressure headache – daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema · Growth failure – downward crossing of height percentiles after a stable channel, weight preserved; endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism keep a normal or increased weight, and in poor nutrition weight loss comes before height loss · Pubertal delay – no breast development by age 13 in girls · Stalk pattern – multiple anterior axes down, with or without posterior failure (diabetes insipidus); stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly growth failure from TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) or growth hormone deficiency; morning cortisol, free T4 (thyroxine), TSH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) come back low in more than one axis · Gland pattern – a single hypersecreting axis with the others intact
Where is the mass
LocationTumorTell
Suprasellar, midlineCraniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; the adamantinomatous type peaks at 5 to 14 and 50 to 74 yearsCystic and calcified; growth failure, pubertal delay, bitemporal hemianopsia; years of subtle symptoms
Suprasellar or pineal, midlineGerminoma (can't miss): germ cell tumor; adolescent, often maleDiabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes; beta-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) usually negative in a pure germinoma, though low beta-hCG can be detected; radiosensitive
IntrasellarProlactinoma or other pituitary adenoma; adolescent or adultNon-calcified; one axis hypersecreting, others intact; galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic features
Optic chiasm or nerveOptic pathway glioma (pilocytic astrocytoma); young child, often NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1)Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with a normal appetite)
SellaRathke cleft cyst: same embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headache
Pituitary stalkLangerhans cell histiocytosis; young childCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk; lytic skull lesions; seborrheic scalp rash
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classicallyCyst with a mural nodule; ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia; falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma; early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, limbs relatively spared; typically hyperdense on CT (computed tomography), with restricted diffusion; seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid)
Fourth ventricleEpendymomaTends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle; calcification and cysts common
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia still ipsilateral: a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
PonsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings: cranial nerve palsy one side (diplopia from an abducens palsy is often first), long-tract weakness the other; diffuse pontine expansion
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia
Occipital lobeSupratentorial massContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema → Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass → height falling while weight holds is endocrine, and Tanner 1 at 14, with the mass signs, suggests a second failed axis, so the stalk is involved; with headache and disc edema the mass is midline and suprasellar, cystic and calcified: craniopharyngioma. A vermian tumor brings truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared, and this examination is clean; subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis, a skin-first diagnosis that does not arrest linear growth
  2. 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → every cerebellar sign is on the left, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the output decussates twice; limb dysmetria is hemispheric, the face is served ipsilaterally, and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. The right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side, and a frontal lobe mass gives contralateral weakness
  3. 9-year-old girl, 2 months of bumping into door frames height fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 55th percentile Misses fingers in the outer field of each eye Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → MRI of the brain with contrast → a height percentile crossing with weight held and loss of the outer field in each eye is a suprasellar mass until imaged: MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views. A bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI, and a noncontrast CT shows the mass and its relation to the chiasm less well than MRI
  4. 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline vermian mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and relatively spared limbs localizes to the vermis; a midline fourth-ventricular mass with restricted diffusion in a child fits medulloblastoma, which seeds drop metastases through the CSF. A cerebellar hemisphere pilocytic astrocytoma gives ipsilateral limb signs and is classically a cyst with a mural nodule; ependymoma tends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle, with calcification and cysts common
  5. 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery Imaging shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → stalk compression can leave several axes deficient, so measure morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery; secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are treated before the operation, glucocorticoid first. Growth hormone does not come before the axes that threaten the operation, and a planned resection is not a reason to wait 6 months for another MRI
  6. 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → a cranial nerve palsy on one side with long-tract weakness on the other is a crossed finding, which localizes to the brainstem; diffuse expansion of the pons in a child is a diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and diplopia from an abducens palsy is often its first sign. Medulloblastoma and a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma give ataxia rather than crossed findings
  7. 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Suprasellar germinoma → diabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes, with a mildly raised CSF beta-hCG and a normal AFP is a suprasellar germinoma (pure germinomas usually have negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected), which is highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy, alone or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Craniopharyngioma is cystic and calcified, and growth hormone and gonadotropin deficits are often its first endocrine failures; Langerhans cell histiocytosis thickens the stalk and brings lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rash
  8. 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → papilledema with cerebellar signs means a posterior fossa mass until imaged, and lumbar puncture risks herniation, so image first: MRI of the brain instead. Measuring an opening pressure does not remove that risk, and a noncontrast CT followed by a tap still ends in the tap that papilledema with a posterior fossa mass forbids
  9. 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min → Desmopressin → dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after the stalk has been handled is central diabetes insipidus: desmopressin. Fluid restriction worsens the hypernatremia, and hypertonic saline adds sodium to a patient whose sodium is already high
  10. 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min → MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markers → upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation are Parinaud syndrome, a pineal-region mass; in an adolescent boy that is classically a germinoma, so obtain MRI of the brain first, then serum and CSF tumor markers, the CSF once imaging shows a tap is safe. This is not strabismus, and a noncontrast CT does not characterize the mass or the markers
  11. 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → hypotension, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with a new suprasellar mass is adrenal crisis; give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline, and avoid levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement, because thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis
  12. 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor → Cerebellar output decussates twice → cerebellar output decussates twice, so the two crossings cancel and the signs stay on the same side as the lesion. Cerebellar fibers do cross, and the cerebellum does not control the opposite limbs directly
  13. 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative → Prolactinoma → galactorrhea and amenorrhea with a raised prolactin, a normal TSH and pregnancy test, and a small, non-calcified intrasellar lesion with one axis hypersecreting is a prolactinoma; cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist. Craniopharyngioma is a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, and a Rathke cleft cyst is a non-enhancing, non-calcified cyst that is usually asymptomatic
  14. 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and a falling level of consciousness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection. Acetazolamide with outpatient follow-up, or observation, leaves the obstruction untreated
  15. 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile → MRI of the brain and orbits → café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling point to neurofibromatosis type 1, and declining vision with emaciation despite a good appetite is an optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome: MRI of the brain and orbits. Celiac disease is malabsorption and brings no visual loss, and a skeletal survey looks for bone lesions he does not have
  16. 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging is MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology, the lumbar puncture done at least 10 to 14 days after surgery. Bone marrow and whole-body imaging do not look where it spreads
  17. 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → a suprasellar mass that blocks CSF flow at the third ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus; a falling level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion. Lumbar puncture risks herniation, and acetazolamide does not relieve an obstruction
  18. 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min → MRI of the brain → headache that wakes him from sleep, with morning vomiting, in a child under six is a red-flag headache: MRI of the brain, because a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor. A diary or migraine prophylaxis delays the diagnosis
  19. 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → a suprasellar mass presses up on the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal fields, decussate: bitemporal hemianopsia. A lesion behind the chiasm, in the optic tract, gives a homonymous defect (the same hemifield lost in both eyes), and a Meyer loop lesion in the temporal lobe gives contralateral superior quadrantanopia
  20. 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → after a craniopharyngioma, surveillance is lifelong and endocrine and visual: serial growth velocity with an annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields. Audiometry does not watch the axes or the visual fields this tumor threatens, and AFP and beta-hCG are germ cell tumor markers
Workup and management
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? If not, the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa. Plot the growth chart: height falling with weight holding is endocrine. Count failed axes: growth and puberty together are panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk. Is there posterior pituitary failure? Polyuria makes germinoma or histiocytosis more likely. Is there raised pressure or a field cut? Papilledema or bitemporal hemianopsia makes the mass midline and suprasellar, and the imaging descriptor is cystic and calcified (calcification mainly on CT). If the examination is focal, find the side, then the structure.
Management Before surgery – treat secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism before the operation, glucocorticoid before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency. Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism. · After surgery – diabetes insipidus can develop in 70% after craniopharyngioma surgery; expect the sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled, and treat hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction · Obstructive hydrocephalus – a posterior fossa mass with drowsiness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection; a suprasellar mass with a depressed level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion, not lumbar puncture · Germinoma – highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy alone, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by response-based radiation therapy, which has been explored to reduce radiation doses and neurodevelopmental harm · Prolactinoma – cabergoline, the preferred dopamine agonist · After craniopharyngioma – lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance, with surveillance MRI
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first.
Reading a sellar vignette Height crossing down through percentiles with weight steady is endocrine growth failure; it excludes undernutrition, which costs weight first. Tanner 1 past age 13 in a girl is delayed puberty; with growth failure and signs of a mass (headache, disc edema), it suggests a second failed axis, which can indicate hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. Optic disc edema without fever or neck stiffness is raised intracranial pressure without meningitis, from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle. A normal neurologic examination, including finger-nose-finger testing and gait, excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma. Normal skin excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists. No focal deficit and no fever exclude brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever. A year of headaches before worsening is a slow-growing lesion, not a reassurance; the normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise. Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging: a height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. The exception to preserved weight is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite. Diabetes insipidus first and anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma; send serum beta-hCG and AFP, and CSF levels once imaging shows a tap is safe, before assuming craniopharyngioma. Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly (height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty) but does not produce papilledema; check TSH and free T4, and disc edema separates the two. Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six. Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.
Common wrong answers Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis and does not arrest linear growth. Tumor in the cerebellar vermis: truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared; it does not touch the pituitary. Parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: abscess is acute, febrile and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection. Enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence. Right middle cerebellar peduncle for left-sided signs: the right region on the wrong side. Pineal mass: common in children, but it produces Parinaud syndrome. Germinoma when the anterior axes failed first and there is no polyuria; adenoma when two axes are down, there is no galactorrhea, and CSF flow is blocked; optic glioma with normal skin, normal pupils and weight preserved; Rathke cleft cyst for progressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure, too much disease for a simple cyst; histiocytosis with normal skin, no polyuria and no bone pain.
Pairs with Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in the opposite direction. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Headache in a School-Age Child: the workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: posterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization. Hyperprolactinemia: the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Polyuria: the step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed?
Transferable rule

When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic: a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema. When the finding is neurologic, localize side first and structure second; the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.

Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child

Kocher criteria count · ultrasound for an effusion · aspirate at 3 or more · transient synovitis vs Perthes by the courseHow many Kocher criteria are present: aspirate now, or treat with NSAIDs and recheck?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A septic hip is a surgical emergency: aspirate before antibiotics.

Count the Kocher criteria:

  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Refuses to bear weight
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) over 40 mm/h
  • WBC (white blood cell count) over 12,000/mm³
  • CRP (C-reactive protein) over 2.0 mg/dL is often added as a fifth

3 or more: blood culture and ultrasound-guided aspiration. 0 or 1: transient synovitis; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and a recheck.

An effusion, and the flexed, abducted, externally rotated hip it causes, occurs in both septic arthritis and transient synovitis; effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis.

Septic fluid (over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant) means surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics.

Diagnosis
Kocher criteria Fever – over 38.5 °C · Weight bearing – refuses · ESR – over 40 mm/h · WBC – over 12,000/mm³ · Score – one point each, unweighted
Kocher criteria ladderProbability of septic arthritis by criteria count
Kocher criteria presentProbability of septic arthritisAction
0under 0.2%Treat as transient synovitis; recheck
1about 3%Observe with close follow-up
2about 40%Gray zone: 2 alone is below the gate; aspirate if toxic
3about 93%Arthrocentesis
4about 99.6%Arthrocentesis; surgical urgency Kocher, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1999 derivation (n=282)
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the painful hip
TierInterventionEscalate when
Kocher 0 to 1Rest and NSAIDs; activity as toleratedFever, refuses to bear weight, or no improvement in 24 to 48 hours
RecheckRepeat CBC, ESR, CRP; re-examine and rescore3 or more criteria, a toxic child with an effusion, or worse
AspirateBlood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration, before antibioticsFluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or purulent
SepticSurgical drainage plus IV antibioticsTop rung
Before you treat Organisms – S aureus overall; Kingella under 4 years; gonococcus in adolescents; Salmonella in sickle cell disease · Delay – femoral head osteonecrosis and growth arrest · Bone, not joint – fever with point tenderness over the metaphysis, motion preserved: osteomyelitis · On methotrexate – one hot joint out of step with the rest is infection until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy with 1 day of right hip pain refuses to bear weight on the right leg cries with any passive movement of the hip No trauma; no recent illness T 39.1 °C · WBC 15,000/mm³ · ESR 62 mm/h → Arthrocentesis → 4 of 4 Kocher criteria (about 99%); draw a blood culture and aspirate before antibiotics
  2. 7-year-old boy with 2 days of left hip pain will not walk; lies with the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated screams with gentle passive rotation No point tenderness over the femur T 39.0 °C · WBC 14,000/mm³ · ESR 90 mm/h → Septic arthritis of the hip → Kocher 4 of 4; the position only shows an effusion (it occurs in transient synovitis too); motion this painful is the joint, not the bone
  3. 4-year-old boy limping since a cold 10 days ago today he refuses to bear weight on the left leg holds the left hip flexed and turned outward T 39.2 °C · ESR 78 mm/h · WBC pending → Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → fever, refusal to bear weight and an ESR over 40 are 3 of 4 with the WBC still pending; a recent cold does not make it benign
  4. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of a limp after a cold 10 days ago walks, favoring the right leg; well appearing T 37.9 °C · WBC 11,500/mm³ · ESR 18 mm/h · CRP 0.8 mg/dL (normal under 1) · ultrasound: effusions in both hips → Transient synovitis → Kocher 0 of 4; an effusion occurs in both diseases, but effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis (septic arthritis is usually one-sided): NSAIDs and a recheck
  5. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of right knee soreness and a limp began after gymnastics practice right knee: full, painless motion, no swelling or tenderness right hip: internal rotation limited and painful Afebrile · bears weight → Ultrasound of both hips → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip, which refers pain to the knee; ultrasound of both hips looks for effusions
  6. 6-year-old girl with 3 days of a left-sided limp well appearing; walks and bears weight mild pain at the end of hip rotation T 37.4 °C · WBC 8,900/mm³ · ESR 12 mm/h · CRP normal · ultrasound: small effusions in both hips → Arthrocentesis of both hips → Kocher 0 of 4: the needle is for 3 or more; treat and recheck
  7. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk ultrasound-guided hip aspiration: cloudy fluid 80,000 WBC/mm³, 90% neutrophils; Gram stain pending Blood culture drawn before the tap T 39.4 °C · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics → fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant: a septic hip is a surgical emergency, and antibiotics alone cannot decompress the joint
  8. 2-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of fever and refusal to bear weight on the left leg screams when the left hip is moved Ultrasound shows a left hip effusion; aspiration is planned T 39.4 °C · WBC 18,000/mm³ → Salmonella → sickle cell disease adds Salmonella to S aureus; Kingella also fits his age, and gonococcus is the adolescent's
  9. 3-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk hip aspirate: purulent, 95,000 WBC/mm³, mostly neutrophils the operating room is not free until tomorrow Started on IV antibiotics after cultures T 39.2 °C · ESR 70 mm/h → Femoral head osteonecrosis → pus under pressure inside the capsule cuts off blood to the femoral head; delay also risks growth arrest
  10. 4-year-old boy with 4 days of a limp and left thigh pain point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis passive hip and knee motion nearly full and only mildly painful Well appearing T 38.6 °C · CRP 6 mg/dL · radiographs normal → Osteomyelitis → fever with point bone tenderness and preserved motion is bone, not joint: MRI; radiographs are normal early
  11. 5-year-old boy treated with ibuprofen for a post-viral limp 4 weeks later he still limps, worse after play hip abduction and internal rotation now limited No fever, night pain or weight loss T 37.0 °C · WBC and ESR normal → Radiographs of both hips → most transient synovitis resolves within 2 weeks; a limp past that needs hip radiographs for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  12. 11-year-old girl with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate wrists, knees and ankles improving 4 days of right shoulder pain, now waking her at night will not move the shoulder T 38.5 °C · synovial fluid 55,000 WBC/mm³, 80% neutrophils → Begin antibiotic therapy → one joint out of step with the rest, with fever and septic fluid on an immunosuppressant: infection, not a flare: antibiotics, then drain the joint; steroid into the joint or more methotrexate would feed it
  13. 4-year-old boy with 1 day of hip pain and a limp cold 10 days ago; no trauma appears well; no bony tenderness hip motion limited by pain Vital signs normal · ultrasound: small right hip effusion · CBC and ESR pending → Ibuprofen and a recheck → afebrile and walking: at most 2 of 4 even if both pending labs return high, and he looks well, so treat and recheck; read the labs when they return; the ultrasound already answered the imaging question, and his pain needs treatment
Pairs with The Limping Child: no hot hip, so match the age and the time. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent who cannot rotate the hip inward.
Transferable rule

A limp alone is not a reason to aspirate: score Kocher first.

Before ordering another test, name the question it answers that the last one did not.
