Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease

cystic fibrosis · primary ciliary dyskinesia · antibody deficiency · foreign body · allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis when antibiotics failWhich exam finding could no immune defect produce, and when an adequate antibiotic course fails, are the eosinophils and immunoglobulin E (IgE) up?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Frequency shows that something is wrong; anatomy shows what. Antibiotic-requiring bacterial sinusitis and pneumonia crosses the gate; up to 12 self-limited viral illnesses a year is normal.

  • Heart on the right: the point of maximal impulse in the right chest is situs inversus; with recurrent sinopulmonary infection, it points to a ciliary defect: primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Kartagener syndrome is PCD with situs inversus, recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis.
  • Poor growth or greasy stools: cystic fibrosis; sweat chloride.
  • Focal and abrupt after choking: a retained foreign body; bronchoscopy.
  • Normal anatomy with absent tonsils or adolescent or adult onset: an antibody defect; quantitative immunoglobulins.
  • Antibiotics fail in a damaged airway: no improvement after a week of adequate antibiotics or unexplained lung-function decline, with eosinophilia and IgE usually above 1,000 international units (IU)/mL, is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), an immune response.
  • Bronchiectasis: the endpoint of any retained secretions, never the cause.
Diagnosis
Recurrent infection: the finding that picks the cause
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
PCD (autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect)Wet cough, otitis and sinusitis from infancy; distress as a term newbornHeart on the right, in 40% to 50%
Cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) defect)Inspissated secretions, repeated infection, bronchiectasisFailure to thrive, greasy stools, meconium ileus, nasal polyps; heart on the left
Retained foreign bodyToddler, abrupt choking episodeFocal wheeze; unilateral hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film
Antibody deficiencyEncapsulated sinopulmonary infection, normal airway anatomyXLA: absent tonsils and adenoids; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID): adolescent or adult onset
Heterotaxy (situs ambiguus)Congenital heart disease, midline liverAsplenia or polysplenia
When antibiotics fail in a structural lung
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisOrganic antigen; fever, malaise, airspace infiltratesImproves in hospital; no eosinophilia, normal IgE
StrongyloidiasisRural tropics or subtropics; eosinophilia, high IgERoaming urticaria, gastrointestinal symptoms
Granulomatosis with polyangiitisNecrotizing bronchiectasis mimicking refractory pneumoniaOlder men; sinus destruction, hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis; no eosinophilia
Nontuberculous mycobacteriaMycobacterium avium complex in cystic fibrosis bronchiectasisMonths to years; nodular, then cavitary; no eosinophilia or IgE rise
Mechanism Dynein arms – the defect makes airway cilia dysmotile and leaves embryonic nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry, so laterality is randomized · Aspergillus – everyone inhales the spores and the mucociliary escalator clears them; a damaged airway (asthma or cystic fibrosis) traps them, and chronic colonization becomes Th2 hypersensitization
Management
By diagnosis PCD – daily airway clearance · ABPA – systemic glucocorticoid first-line; an antifungal such as voriconazole is added to reduce spore burden; an antifungal alone treats the antigen, not the response · Eosinophilia with tropical exposure – screen for and treat strongyloidiasis before systemic steroids, which can progress it to hyperinfection or dissemination · Heterotaxy with asplenia – encapsulated-organism prophylaxis · Cystic fibrosis – annual total IgE screens for ABPA
Practice
  1. 11-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a week of fever and productive cough no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia IgE 3,225 IU/mL No travel, rash or gastrointestinal symptoms T 38.4°C · bilateral crackles → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → antibiotic failure plus eosinophilia and an IgE more than triple the usual threshold make it allergic, not bacterial. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis improves in hospital and gives no eosinophilia and a normal IgE; granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects older adults, without eosinophilia
  2. 3-year-old girl has had a chronic wet cough since infancy recurrent otitis media since infancy chest film: cardiac silhouette on the right stomach bubble on the right Growth normal for age Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% → Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) → a heart on the right with chronic wet cough and otitis points to a ciliary defect: the dynein-arm defect leaves nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry. Without normal ciliary function during embryogenesis, abnormal orientation can result; cystic fibrosis does not involve this defect; heterotaxy is situs ambiguus with asplenia or polysplenia and heart disease. Confirm with nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary electron microscopy
  3. 15-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has an exacerbation that fails initial therapy sputum grows Pseudomonas resistant to the current antibiotic eosinophil count normal IgE normal T 38.3°C · oxygen saturation 93% → Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivities → a resistant organism with normal eosinophils and IgE is still a bacterial exacerbation: adjust to culture sensitivities. Without the allergic markers, neither glucocorticoids nor repeat Aspergillus serology fits
  4. 2-year-old boy has his third pneumonia this year chronic loose, greasy stools weight below the 3rd percentile point of maximal impulse in the left chest No choking episode; tonsils present T 38.6°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Sweat chloride testing → with the heart on the left, poor growth and greasy stools open the cystic fibrosis axis: sweat chloride, 60 mmol/L or more. Immunoglobulins fit normal anatomy without tonsils; nasal nitric oxide fits a ciliary picture with normal growth
  5. 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis this week Aspergillus-specific IgE positive CT: mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Productive cough despite a week of antibiotics T 37.9°C · total IgE 2,600 IU/mL → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → the pathology is allergic inflammation: a systemic glucocorticoid first-line, with an antifungal added to reduce spore burden. Voriconazole alone treats the antigen, not the response; more antibacterial coverage treats an infection that is not there
  6. 14-month-old boy choked while eating nuts 3 weeks ago now a focal right-sided wheeze second right lower lobe pneumonia film: right-sided hyperinflation Well before the choking episode T 38.2°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Rigid bronchoscopy → abrupt onset after choking, focal wheeze and unilateral hyperinflation are a retained foreign body: rigid bronchoscopy finds and removes it. Another antibiotic course or a CT leaves the obstruction in place
  7. 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes for her routine annual review feels well baseline cough unchanged No wheeze or new sputum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · lung function at her baseline → Total serum IgE → cystic fibrosis earns an annual total serum IgE, one of the few purely serologic screening intervals; CT and skin testing are not the yearly screen
  8. 5-year-old boy has had recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age no palpable tonsils no cervical lymphadenopathy Heart sounds loudest in the left chest; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometry → normal anatomy with absent lymphoid tissue is the antibody axis; all immunoglobulins low with B cells absent is X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Sweat chloride needs poor growth or greasy stools, and ciliary biopsy needs a ciliary picture
  9. 45-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has several months of cough and weight loss CT: nodular and cavitary opacities No hemoptysis; no recent travel eosinophils 2% · IgE 90 IU/mL · oxygen saturation 94% → Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease → cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex, rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis: chronic over months to years, nodular then cavitary. No eosinophilia or IgE rise removes the allergic cause
  10. 8-year-old boy has a year-round wet cough unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn chronic otitis media point of maximal impulse in the left chest Growth and stools normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Nasal nitric oxide measurement → situs inversus appears in only 40% to 50% of PCD, so a heart on the left does not exclude it; low nasal nitric oxide supports PCD with normal situs. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and a repeat film adds nothing
  11. 34-year-old woman has asthma that is difficult to control recurrent brown mucus plugs central bronchiectasis on CT IgE 2,400 IU/mL Aspergillus skin test positive T 37.2°C · peripheral eosinophilia · oxygen saturation 95% → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → same disease, different structural host: asthma, like cystic fibrosis, traps the spores. A systemic glucocorticoid with an antifungal; more inhaled steroid or antibacterial therapy leaves the allergic response untreated
  12. 3-year-old girl in daycare has had 9 upper respiratory illnesses this year each self-limited without antibiotics normal examination between illnesses Older brother is well growth at the 50th percentile · Afebrile → Normal frequency of childhood viral infection → up to 12 viral illnesses a year is normal in daycare or with older siblings: reassure, no immune workup. Ciliary disease and antibody defects give antibiotic-requiring bacterial infection, not colds that clear alone
  13. 52-year-old man who farms has fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates no response to a week of antibiotics symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital No travel or rash IgE 40 IU/mL · eosinophils 1% → Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposure → improvement in hospital, away from the exposure, with a normal IgE and no eosinophilia is hypersensitivity pneumonitis: identify and eliminate the antigen, since removal from the exposure is what brings improvement. The allergic fungal disease needs eosinophilia and a high IgE, and the improvement already explains the picture without a biopsy
  14. 18-month-old boy has had 8 antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia older brother has the same illness mildly enlarged tonsils point of maximal impulse in the right chest Delivered vaginally without complications oxygen saturation 99% · bilateral rales and rhonchi → Primary ciliary dyskinesia → the heart on the right decides: visceral rotation needs normal ciliary movement, which an antibody defect leaves intact. Tonsils exclude X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and 18 months excludes CVID; bilateral rales with a normal saturation argue against a foreign body; the affected brother alone separates none of them
  15. 40-year-old man from the rural tropics has refractory pulmonary infiltrates migratory urticaria abdominal pain IgE 4,100 IU/mL Infiltrates persist after 10 days of antibiotics T 37.8°C · eosinophils 18% · oxygen saturation 94% → Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoids → eosinophilia and a high IgE with roaming urticaria, gut symptoms and tropical exposure are strongyloidiasis: treat it before any systemic glucocorticoid, which risks hyperinfection or dissemination. Antituberculous therapy explains neither the eosinophilia nor the urticaria
  16. 4-year-old boy adopted at 6 months has 6 months of nasal obstruction recurrent nosebleeds repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia bilateral nasal polyps; digital clubbing Diffuse coarse crackles weight 3rd, height 5th percentile · oxygen saturation 93% → Cystic fibrosis → nasal polyps, clubbing and poor growth with recurrent infection point to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride testing; newborn screening misses rarer CFTR mutations. Allergic rhinitis causes neither poor growth nor clubbing, and a vasculitis explains neither in a 4-year-old with recurrent sinopulmonary infection
  17. 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 2 weeks of productive cough no improvement after 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia total IgE 1,850 IU/mL No travel or rash Afebrile · oxygen saturation 95% → Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testing → total IgE suggests; Aspergillus-specific IgE or a skin test confirms sensitization. A sputum culture or galactomannan looks for the fungus, but everyone inhales it: the disease is the immune response
  18. 17-year-old boy has had sinusitis all his life chronic productive cough infertility evaluation with his partner semen analysis: normal sperm count, absent motility No greasy stools; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defects → a normal count with absent motility is the ciliary pattern, and electron microscopy shows the dynein-arm defect. Cystic fibrosis often gives obstructive azoospermia or severe oligospermia from congenital absence of the vas deferens, which a normal count excludes. Klinefelter syndrome typically gives small testes with reduced testosterone, not a normal count with immotile sperm, and no sinusitis
  19. 13-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis sputum has grown Aspergillus repeatedly IgE 2,900 IU/mL Neutrophil count normal; no cavity on CT Afebrile · eosinophils 12% · oxygen saturation 96% → Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitization → everyone inhales the spores, and the mucociliary escalator clears them; trapped mucus allows colonization, then Th2 sensitization. A normal neutrophil count and no cavity remove the other two
  20. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with primary ciliary dyskinesia at age 4 daily purulent sputum high-resolution CT: lower-lobe bronchiectasis crackles at both lung bases Takes no maintenance therapy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Begin daily airway clearance therapy → the bronchiectasis comes from failed mucociliary clearance, so start daily airway clearance; antibiotics only during exacerbations leave the secretions in place, and resection removes one lobe of a disease of the whole airway
  21. 10-year-old girl has had two pneumococcal bacteremias midline liver complex congenital heart disease no spleen on abdominal imaging Growth normal; no chronic wet cough Afebrile · HR 96/min · oxygen saturation 96% → Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxis → situs ambiguus with no spleen is the asplenia of heterotaxy: protect against encapsulated organisms with vaccination and daily prophylaxis. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and airway clearance a ciliary one
  22. 4-year-old boy has a chronic wet cough recurrent otitis media recurrent sinusitis since infancy chest film: situs inversus totalis Growth normal; tonsils present; stools normal Afebrile · HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 97% → Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme → dynein arms power ciliary beating; their defect impairs mucociliary clearance and randomizes laterality. CFTR and Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause infection without the ciliary dysfunction that misplaces the heart
  23. 6-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has recurrent nosebleeds greasy, foul-smelling stools weight below the 3rd percentile repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia Bruises easily on the shins platelets 280,000/mm³ · prothrombin time prolonged → Pancreatic insufficiency with vitamin K malabsorption → pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins, and vitamin K deficiency causes the bleeding; neither sinus inflammation nor platelet dysfunction prolongs the prothrombin time
Common wrong answers XLA with tonsils present: it has no tonsillar or adenoidal tissue. CVID at 18 months: it presents in adolescence or adulthood. Normal childhood infection: those are viral and need no antibiotics; eight antibiotic courses are a disease pattern. Fever as proof of infection: fever, malaise and blood-streaked sputum are common in ABPA. Broader antibiotics: antibiotic failure is a finding, not a dosing problem; change the category (allergic, mycobacterial, vasculitic) before the spectrum. Tuberculosis: cystic fibrosis airways are colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria.
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies: the airway is structurally normal, so immunoglobulin levels and the B-cell count decide. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies: what pancreatic insufficiency does to vitamins A, D, E and K; is the prothrombin time long? Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult with brown mucus plugs.
Transferable rule

A physical finding that no immune defect could produce decides the cause of recurrent infection. When a treatment that should work fails, the failure is the finding: change the category of disease, most often infection to hypersensitivity, rather than intensifying treatment.
